parts.title: Hiring a van for a house move

turns.text: Good morning, Kingsway Van Hire, Simon speaking. How can I help?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Oh, hi. I'm moving into a new flat next weekend, and I'd like to hire a van, please.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely. Let me just take a few details first. Could I have your name?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Yes, it's Megan Holroyd. Holroyd is H-O-L-R-O-Y-D.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thanks, Megan. And what size van were you thinking of? We've got small, medium and large.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Well, I was going to go for the small one, because it's only a one-bedroom flat. But I've got a sofa and a double bed, so I'm not sure they'd fit.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Honestly, with a sofa and a bed, the small one would be a real squeeze. The next size up has a much longer loading space, and it's still easy to drive. The large one's really for moving a whole house.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Right. I'll take your advice and go for the medium one, then.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Good choice. And when would you like to pick it up?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: I was hoping for Friday evening, but my friend who's helping me can't get off work, so it'll have to be Saturday morning.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's no problem, we've still got medium vans free that weekend. What time would suit you?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: As early as possible, really. Do you open at eight?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The office opens at eight, yes, but every van has to be checked and cleaned first. So the earliest you can collect it is 8.30.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: OK, 8.30 it is. That still gives us most of the day.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Great. Now, we also need the address you're moving to, for our insurance.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: It's Flat 4, 27 Lindley Road. That's L-I-N-D-L-E-Y.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thank you. Is that the one near the hospital?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: That's right, just behind it. It's only about ten minutes from my old place, actually.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Handy. And could I have a contact number, in case we need to get hold of you?
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Yes, my mobile is 07700 900 326. Oh, sorry, I always mix that up. The last part is 362.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: So that's 07700 900 362. Got it.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Now, how much will it cost? I saw on your website that the medium van was £65 a day.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's our weekday price, I'm afraid. At weekends it's a bit more, so it'd be £75 for the Saturday. But if you keep it until Sunday, we do a special deal.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Actually, I might need it on Sunday as well, to take some old furniture to the tip.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: In that case, the weekend rate is £110 for both days, which works out cheaper than paying for two separate days.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Right, that sounds fine. Let's do that.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely. Would you like any extras? We hire out trolleys for £8, and furniture blankets for £5.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: I've already borrowed a trolley from my neighbour, so I won't need one. But the blankets would be useful. I don't want to scratch anything.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: I'll add those to the booking. Now, there's also a deposit, which you get back when the van's returned without any damage. It used to be £200, but it's now £150.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: OK, that's not too bad. And what do I need to bring with me when I collect it?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Your driving licence, obviously, and something with your address on it. A bank statement isn't enough, I'm afraid. It needs to be a recent bill, like gas or electricity.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Oh, but it'll still have my old address on it. Is that a problem?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: No, that's fine, as long as it matches the address on your licence.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Good. And how long does it all take at the office? I don't want my friend waiting around.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Most people expect it to take about ten minutes, but with the checks and the photos of the van, you should allow about twenty minutes.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Twenty. OK, I'll tell her. And when I bring it back on Sunday, is there anything I need to do?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: You'll need to return it by six in the evening. And please make sure the tank's full before you drop it off, otherwise there's a £30 refuelling charge.
turns.speaker: staff

turns.text: Right, I'll stop at the petrol station on the way. Thanks so much for your help.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: You're welcome, Megan. Good luck with the move.
turns.speaker: staff

explanation.uk: Офіс відчиняється о восьмій, але фургони спершу треба перевірити й почистити, тож забрати його вона зможе о "8.30", а не о "eight".

explanation.uk: Абонентка називає свою нову адресу і диктує назву вулиці по літерах: "L-I-N-D-L-E-Y".

questions.prompt: Mobile number: 07700 900 ______

explanation.en: She first says 326 by mistake, then corrects it to 362, and the assistant repeats the number to check it.
explanation.ru: Сначала она по ошибке говорит "326", затем исправляется на "362", и сотрудник повторяет номер, чтобы его проверить.
explanation.uk: Спочатку вона помилково каже "326", потім виправляє на "362", і співробітник повторює номер, щоб його перевірити.

parts.title: Welcome to Riverbend Botanic Gardens

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverbend Botanic Gardens. My name's Aroha Tremain, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you head off on your own, I'll quickly explain where everything is, and then I'll tell you what's on this month. You've each got a map, so have a look at that as I go.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right. We're standing at the main gate, at the bottom of your map. The main path runs straight north from here, right up through the middle of the gardens. As you walk up it, the first building on your right is the Visitor Centre. That's where you'll find information and our gift shop.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, a lot of people assume the café's in the Visitor Centre too, but it isn't. It's directly across the path from it, on your left as you walk north, right next to the Rose Garden. They do a lovely flat white, if you need one.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Keep going and you'll reach a crossroads, where a second path runs from east to west. Now, the toilets. If you turn right at the crossroads and walk all the way to the end of that path, they're on your right-hand side. They're the only toilets in the gardens, by the way, so it's worth remembering where they are.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: On the other side of the path, facing the toilets, is the herb garden. It's a favourite with keen cooks, and you're welcome to touch and smell the plants. Just please don't pick them!
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, back to the crossroads. If you carry straight on north, the building immediately on your left is the Fernery. It's cool and shady in there, so it's a nice escape on a warm day. The building opposite it, on the right, is the staff office, and I'm afraid that's not open to visitors.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: If you've got children with you, they'll want the children's garden. For that, go to the crossroads and turn left, so you're heading west. Walk to the very end of the path, and it's on your right, just south of the Duck Pond. There's a sandpit and a little hedge maze in there.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Last one. The plant shop sells seedlings grown in our own nursery, and it's well worth a visit. Go right to the top of the main path, where you'll see the big Glasshouse. The shop's in the small building just to the east of it, so that's on your right as you face the Glasshouse.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, so that's where everything is. Now, what's on this month. We run free guided walks every day. They used to leave at 10:30 am, but this month they start at 11 am, from just outside the Visitor Centre. Do try to get there ten minutes early, though, because they fill up fast.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: In the Glasshouse, we'd planned to have our orchid display this month, but the orchids are flowering late this year, so that's been moved to January. Instead, there's a special exhibition of carnivorous plants, the ones that trap insects. The cactus collection's in there all year round, of course.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: A few people have asked about the Rose Garden. It's open as usual, but don't expect too much just yet. Most of the roses are still in bud, and they won't be at their best until about mid-December.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, this Saturday there's a gardening workshop. Lots of people ask us about pruning, but we do that one in winter. This one's all about growing vegetables from seed, and everyone takes home a tray of seedlings. Next month's workshop is on composting, if that's more your thing.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: It's $15 per person, and there are only twenty places. Please don't try to book on our website, because the booking form isn't working this week. We can't take bookings over the phone, either. Just pop into the Visitor Centre and put your name down at the desk.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: And finally, on Sunday, sorry, Friday evening, there's a twilight concert on the lawn by the Duck Pond. You don't need to bring chairs, we've got plenty, and the paths will be lit, so leave your torch at home. But it does get chilly once the sun goes down, so bring an extra layer.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, that's all from me. Enjoy your visit, and if you've got any questions, come and find me. I'll be by the café.
turns.speaker: guide

questions.prompt: Café
questions.evidence: It's directly across the path from it, on your left as you walk north, right next to the Rose Garden.

explanation.en: The café is not inside the Visitor Centre. It is opposite it, on the left as you walk north from the gate, next to the Rose Garden.
explanation.ru: Кафе находится не внутри "Visitor Centre", а напротив него: слева, если идти от ворот на север, рядом с "Rose Garden".
explanation.uk: Кафе розташоване не всередині "Visitor Centre", а навпроти нього: ліворуч, якщо йти від воріт на північ, поруч із "Rose Garden".

questions.prompt: Toilets
questions.evidence: turn right at the crossroads and walk all the way to the end of that path, they're on your right-hand side

explanation.en: Turning right at the crossroads means walking east. At the end of the path, the right-hand side is the south side, so the toilets are B, not the building on the north side.
explanation.ru: Повернуть направо на перекрёстке значит идти на восток. В конце дорожки правая сторона — южная, поэтому туалеты — это B, а не здание на северной стороне.
explanation.uk: Повернути праворуч на перехресті означає йти на схід. Наприкінці доріжки права сторона — південна, тож туалети — це B, а не будівля на північному боці.

questions.prompt: Herb garden
questions.evidence: On the other side of the path, facing the toilets, is the herb garden.

explanation.en: The herb garden is opposite the toilets, on the north side of the east end of the cross path.
explanation.ru: Сад пряных трав находится напротив туалетов, на северной стороне восточного конца поперечной дорожки.
explanation.uk: Сад пряних трав розташований навпроти туалетів, на північному боці східного кінця поперечної доріжки.

questions.prompt: Fernery
questions.evidence: If you carry straight on north, the building immediately on your left is the Fernery.

explanation.en: Going straight on north from the crossroads, the left side is west, so the Fernery is C. The building on the right is the staff office.
explanation.ru: Если от перекрёстка идти прямо на север, слева будет запад, поэтому "Fernery" — это C. Здание справа — служебный офис персонала.
explanation.uk: Якщо від перехрестя йти прямо на північ, ліворуч буде захід, тому "Fernery" — це C. Будівля праворуч — службовий офіс персоналу.

questions.prompt: Children's garden
questions.evidence: Walk to the very end of the path, and it's on your right, just south of the Duck Pond.

explanation.en: Turning left at the crossroads means walking west. At the very end, on the right (north) side and just below the Duck Pond, is the children's garden. You pass the Fernery on the way, but that is not at the end.
explanation.ru: Повернуть налево на перекрёстке значит идти на запад. В самом конце, справа (с северной стороны), прямо под "Duck Pond", находится детский сад-парк для детей. По пути вы проходите мимо "Fernery", но это ещё не конец дорожки.
explanation.uk: Повернути ліворуч на перехресті означає йти на захід. У самому кінці, праворуч (з північного боку), одразу під "Duck Pond", розташований сад для дітей. Дорогою ви проходите повз "Fernery", але це ще не кінець доріжки.

parts.title: Planning a student travel survey

turns.text: Come in, Shannon, Mitchell. Have a seat. So, this is your survey on how students travel to campus. Remind me why you settled on that topic?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Well, we both drive in from out past Penrith, so we know the problem first-hand. But honestly, that wasn't the main reason.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No. The main thing was that the uni's deciding at the moment whether to build another multi-storey car park or spend the money on a shuttle bus, and we thought our results might actually feed into that.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's a good motivation. There's already plenty of research on student travel, so a link to a real decision helps. Now, you ran a pilot. How did that go?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Better than we expected in some ways. We were worried the wording would confuse people, but nobody asked us what anything meant.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The real problem was the time. It took most people about twelve minutes, and a couple just gave up halfway through.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Twelve minutes is a lot to ask of someone between lectures. So you cut it down?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Yes, from twenty-two questions to fourteen. It's about five minutes now.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Good. And how have you been finding participants?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We started by standing outside the library with a clipboard, but that was pretty slow. We only got fifteen or so in two afternoons.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: We also asked a few lecturers to mention it at the start of class, but they said they weren't allowed to. So in the end we put a link on the student union's online noticeboard, and that's where nearly all our responses have come from.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I see. And how many have you got so far?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We set ourselves a target of 150. Last Friday we had about 60, and now we're up to 110.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's healthy. But I do have a concern about who's answering. Have you looked at the breakdown?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We checked faculties, and it's a fairly even spread. Science, arts, business, all roughly the same. And we left out anyone living in the residential colleges, since they don't really travel.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sensible. But think about who reads the union noticeboard. It's mostly full-time students who are on campus every day. People studying part-time, often in the evenings, are hardly represented at all, and they're the group most likely to drive in after work.

turns.text: Right, that's true. We've only got about six part-timers. Could we offer a prize? Like a draw for a $100 voucher?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.speaker: tutor

turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I wouldn't. People are tired and in a hurry, and you'd need permission from campus security. The simplest thing is to email the coordinators of the evening courses and ask them to forward the link to their students.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Okay, we'll do that this week.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. Now, I've been through your fourteen questions, and I've got a few suggestions. The first one asks for their main way of getting here, and they tick one box. But lots of people catch a train and then cycle from the station, or drive to a park-and-ride.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: So we should add more options to the list?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, your list's fine as it is. The issue is that people need to be able to tick more than one.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Okay. Then there's the one on weekly travel costs.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yes. You ask for an exact dollar amount, and I suspect most people have no idea what they spend. Give them bands instead, say under $20, $20 to $40, and so on.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: What about postcode? A few people in the pilot didn't like giving it, so we thought about dropping it altogether.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: And the question on why people chose their transport?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.speaker: tutor

turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: An example might lead them. I'd turn it into a rating scale, from one to five, so you can compare the answers easily.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: So we lose one and gain one. That keeps us at fourteen, then.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. Send me the revised version by Friday, and we'll meet again next week.

segments.text: Part 4. You will hear a university lecturer giving a talk about how honeybees communicate where food can be found. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

parts.title: How honeybees share the location of food

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at a question that puzzled people for a very long time: how does a honeybee that's found food tell the rest of the colony where it is? The answer, or most of it anyway, is a behavior called the waggle dance. And at the end we'll look at the limits of that idea, because it's not quite as neat as the textbooks suggest.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's start with Karl von Frisch, the Austrian biologist who did the classic work on this. He wanted to control exactly where the bees found food, and real flowers are very hard to control. So instead he trained bees to visit a small dish of sugar water, which he could move around the countryside wherever he liked.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Of course, he needed to know which bee was which. He considered clipping a tiny piece off their wings, but that would've changed the way they flew. So he marked each visitor with a little dot of paint, using different colors in a kind of code.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then he watched what those bees did back home. A normal hive is dark and closed, so he used what's called an observation hive. That's basically a frame of comb with glass sides, so you can see what's going on inside without disturbing anyone.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What he saw were two different dances. If the food was close to the hive, within about fifty meters, the returning bee ran around in small circles, first one way, then the other. He called this the round dance. It basically says, there's food nearby, go and look, without giving much detail.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: For food farther away, the bee performs the waggle dance. She runs in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side, then loops back around and repeats it. Now, the direction of that straight run is the clever part.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: On the vertical comb, straight up stands for the direction of the sun. So if the bee waggles at, say, forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food is forty degrees to the right of the sun. Not magnetic north, not the hive entrance. The sun.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What about distance? A lot of students assume it's shown by how fast the bee shakes. Actually, the speed of the waggling hardly changes. It's the duration of the waggle run, how long it lasts, that tells the others how far to fly. So a longer run simply means a longer flight.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: As a rough guide, one second of waggling means the food's about 750 meters away. You'll see some books say a kilometer, but it varies between colonies, so treat it as approximate. Food two kilometers off might get a waggle run of nearly three seconds.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, remember it's pitch black inside a hive, so the other bees can't actually see any of this. Instead, they follow close behind the dancer, pick up the vibrations, and keep touching her body with their antennae. They also pick up the scent of the flowers she's been visiting, which helps them later on.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So how do we know the dance really works like this? Von Frisch's evidence came from watching which feeding sites new bees turned up at. A stronger test came in the late 1980s, sorry, the early 1990s, when a team in Denmark built a robot bee. It was about the size of a real one, made of brass and driven by a computer. When it danced in the hive, real bees flew off to the spot its dance pointed to.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Another test used radar. Researchers fixed tiny transponders to bees that had just followed a dance, then tracked their flights across open fields. Most flew off in roughly the direction the dance had shown, although many still had to search around once they got there.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There's also the question of how a bee measures distance in the first place. Researchers in Australia trained bees to fly down a narrow tunnel with patterned walls to reach food. Afterwards, the bees danced as if they'd flown many times farther than they really had. So they judge distance from how fast the world moves past their eyes, not from how tired they get.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, finally, the limits. The dance is impressive, but it's not the whole story. When researchers watched hives closely, they found that a lot of experienced foragers ignore dances most of the time. They'd rather go back to places they know, relying on their memory of sites that worked before, along with smell.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Other experiments deliberately scrambled the dance, by laying the comb flat and keeping the hive dark, so the direction information was lost. In many temperate habitats, those colonies collected about as much food as normal ones. The dance only made a clear difference where food comes in rare, rich patches, as in tropical forest.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So the waggle dance is real, and it's remarkable. But it's one tool among several, and how much it matters depends on where the bees live. Next week, we'll see how ants solve the same problem using chemical trails.
turns.speaker: lecturer

groups.title: The honeybee waggle dance

questions.prompt: Von Frisch's method: bees trained to feed from a ______ of sugar water instead of real flowers
questions.evidence: he trained bees to visit a small dish of sugar water

explanation.en: The lecturer says real flowers were hard to control, so von Frisch used a small dish of sugar water that he could move around.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что с настоящими цветами было трудно работать, поэтому von Frisch использовал небольшую тарелочку с "sugar water" (сахарной водой), которую можно было переставлять с места на место.
explanation.uk: Лектор каже, що зі справжніми квітами було важко працювати, тож von Frisch використовував невелику мисочку з "sugar water" (цукровою водою), яку міг переставляти з місця на місце.

questions.prompt: Each bee identified by a mark of ______ in a color code

explanation.en: He thought about clipping the wings but rejected the idea because it would change how the bees flew. He used dots of paint instead.
explanation.ru: Он думал о том, чтобы подрезать пчёлам крылья, но отказался от этой идеи: это изменило бы то, как они летают. Вместо этого он ставил на них точки краской ("paint").
explanation.uk: Він думав про те, щоб підрізати бджолам крила, але відмовився від цієї ідеї: це змінило б те, як вони літають. Натомість він ставив на них цятки фарбою ("paint").

questions.prompt: Dances watched in an observation hive with ______ sides
questions.evidence: a frame of comb with glass sides

explanation.en: An observation hive is a frame of comb with glass sides, so people can see inside without disturbing the bees.
explanation.ru: "Observation hive" — это рамка с сотами и стеклянными стенками ("glass"), поэтому можно заглянуть внутрь, не беспокоя пчёл.
explanation.uk: "Observation hive" — це рамка із сотами та скляними стінками ("glass"), тож можна зазирнути всередину, не турбуючи бджіл.

questions.prompt: Round dance: means the food is ______ to the hive
questions.evidence: If the food was close to the hive, within about fifty meters

explanation.en: The round dance is used when food is close to the hive, within about fifty meters. The waggle dance is used for food farther away.
explanation.ru: "Round dance" используется, когда корм находится близко к улью — примерно в пределах "fifty meters". "Waggle dance" — когда корм дальше.
explanation.uk: "Round dance" використовується, коли корм розташований близько до вулика — приблизно в межах "fifty meters". "Waggle dance" — коли корм далі.

questions.prompt: Waggle dance: angle of the straight run from vertical shows direction in relation to the ______
questions.evidence: straight up stands for the direction of the sun

explanation.en: Straight up on the comb stands for the sun's direction. The lecturer says it is not magnetic north or the hive entrance.
explanation.ru: Направление строго вверх по сотам обозначает направление на солнце ("sun"). Лектор уточняет, что это не магнитный север и не вход в улей.
explanation.uk: Напрямок точно вгору по сотах позначає напрямок на сонце ("sun"). Лектор уточнює, що це не магнітна північ і не вхід до вулика.

questions.prompt: Distance is shown by the ______ of the waggle run
questions.evidence: It's the duration of the waggle run, how long it lasts

explanation.en: Many students think the speed of shaking shows distance, but the lecturer says speed hardly changes. It is the duration, or how long the run lasts.
explanation.ru: Многие студенты думают, что расстояние показывает скорость покачиваний, но лектор говорит, что скорость почти не меняется. Важна "duration" — то есть сколько длится этот пробег.
explanation.uk: Багато студентів думають, що відстань показує швидкість похитувань, але лектор каже, що швидкість майже не змінюється. Важить "duration" — тобто скільки триває цей пробіг.

questions.prompt: One second of waggling ≈ food about ______ meters away
questions.evidence: one second of waggling means the food's about 750 meters away

explanation.en: One second means about 750 meters. A kilometer is what some books say, and two kilometers is a separate example.
explanation.ru: Одна секунда соответствует примерно "750" метрам. Километр — это то, что пишут в некоторых книгах, а два километра — отдельный пример.
explanation.uk: Одна секунда відповідає приблизно "750" метрам. Кілометр — це те, що пишуть у деяких книжках, а два кілометри — окремий приклад.

questions.prompt: Hive is dark, so followers stay in contact with the dancer using their ______
questions.evidence: keep touching her body with their antennae

explanation.en: The other bees can't see the dance in the dark, so they feel vibrations and keep touching the dancer with their antennae.
explanation.ru: В темноте другие пчёлы не видят танца, поэтому они ощущают вибрации ("vibrations") и постоянно касаются танцующей пчелы усиками ("antennae").
explanation.uk: У темряві інші бджоли не бачать танцю, тому вони відчувають вібрації ("vibrations") і постійно торкаються бджоли, що танцює, вусиками ("antennae").

questions.prompt: Danish team: a computer-driven ______ bee sent real bees to a chosen spot
questions.evidence: a team in Denmark built a robot bee

explanation.en: In the early 1990s, a team in Denmark built a robot bee made of brass and driven by a computer. Real bees flew where its dance pointed.
explanation.ru: В начале 1990-х команда в Дании ("Denmark") построила пчелу-робота из латуни ("brass"), которой управлял компьютер. Настоящие пчёлы летели туда, куда указывал её танец.
explanation.uk: На початку 1990-х команда в Данії ("Denmark") створила бджолу-робота з латуні ("brass"), якою керував комп'ютер. Справжні бджоли летіли туди, куди вказував її танець.

questions.prompt: Flights of bees that had followed a dance were tracked using ______
questions.evidence: Another test used radar.

explanation.en: Researchers put tiny transponders on bees and tracked them by radar. Most flew in roughly the direction the dance showed.

parts.title: Joining a community choir

turns.text: Good morning, Westgate Community Centre, Craig speaking.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Oh, hi Craig. I'm ringing about the community choir. I'd really love to join, if you're still taking new people.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We certainly are. I actually run the choir, so you've come to the right person. I'll just take a few details first, if that's okay. Can I have your name?
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Sure. It's Fiona Kellaway.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Is that with a C or a K at the start?
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: A K. It's Kellaway, K-E-L-L-A-W-A-Y.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely, thanks. I'll make sure that goes on your name tag correctly, because we had a bit of a mix-up last week. And what's your home address, Fiona?
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: I'm at 27 Gilmour Road, in Yarraville. Gilmour is G-I-L-M-O-U-R.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Got it. 27 Gilmour Road. And what's the best number to reach you on?
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: My mobile's best, because I'm hardly ever home. It's 0431 772 856, sorry, 865.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: So that's 0431 772 865. Great. Now, do you know what voice part you sing? We've got sopranos, altos, tenors and basses.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Well, I always used to put myself down as a soprano, but honestly, I struggle with the really high notes. My old choir leader said I was much more comfortable lower down.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Then we'll put you down as alto for now. We can always try your voice at the first rehearsal and move you if we need to.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: That sounds sensible.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: And have you sung in a choir before? It's not a problem if you haven't. Plenty of our members are complete beginners.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Yes, but it was a long time ago. People always assume it was at school, but our school didn't actually have a choir. I sang in the church choir in my town for about five years as a teenager.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's great experience. One last question for the form. How did you hear about us? We like to know which advertising actually works.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Well, my sister mentioned there was a choir somewhere around here, but she didn't know where it met. Then I saw a poster on the noticeboard at the library, and it had your number on it.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Good to know. We only put those up last month, so I'm glad someone's reading them.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: So when do you rehearse?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: It used to be Tuesday nights, but quite a few members had trouble getting here then. So since February we've moved to Thursday evenings. We start at seven and finish at nine, in the main hall.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Right. That's fine for me. Do I need to bring anything along?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Just a pencil, so you can mark your music. We hand out a folder with all the songs, so you don't need to buy anything. Oh, and bring a water bottle. The hall gets very warm, and singing for two hours is thirsty work.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: I can imagine. And what are the fees?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We charge by the term. It was $80 last year, but the cost of hiring the hall went up, so it's now $90 a term. That covers your sheet music as well.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: That's reasonable. Is there a discount for students? My daughter might want to come too.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Yes, students pay $60 a term, so she'd save a bit.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Good. And can I pay by card when I come in?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Ah, normally yes, but the card machine at the front desk is broken at the moment, and we're still waiting on a new one. So for now it's cash at the desk, or you can pay online through our website.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: No worries. I'll just bring it with me on the night.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Now, we've got two concerts coming up. The second one's our Christmas concert in December, but the first is the winter concert on the twenty-first of June.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Is that held here at the centre?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We did it here last year, but the hall was far too small for all the families. So this year it's going to be at the town hall in Footscray. There's much more room.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Oh, that'll be nice. And is there a uniform for the concerts?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Nothing fancy. Black trousers or a black skirt. A few people asked about wearing blue on top, but we decided a white top looks better under the lights. And we'll give you a red scarf on the night.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Easy enough. I've got all of that already. So I just turn up next Thursday?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's right. Come about ten minutes early and I'll introduce you to the other altos.
turns.speaker: organiser

turns.text: Perfect. Thanks so much, Craig. See you then.
turns.speaker: caller

parts.title: Briefing for festival staff

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Larkmoor Music Festival. My name's Claire Hollis, and I'm the staff manager, so for the next four days I'm the person you'll see running around with a clipboard. Before we hand out uniforms, I want to go through a few things: the jobs, your shifts, the rules, and who to contact when something goes wrong. It shouldn't take more than a quarter of an hour.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Right, jobs first. Most of you applied for a particular role, and we've tried to give everyone what they asked for. Bar work, for example, is completely full now, and so is ticket scanning at the entrance gates, so we won't be moving anyone into those teams.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Where we're really short is in the car parks, directing the traffic, and in the recycling team, picking up litter. Most visitors arrive on Thursday afternoon, sorry, Friday afternoon, so that's when the car parks are busiest. Litter picking isn't glamorous, I know, but it's often the job people enjoy most by Sunday. The information tents, on the other hand, have more than enough volunteers already.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Okay, shifts. Each one is six hours, not eight, as it said in some of the old adverts. You need to sign in at the crew check-in tent at least fifteen minutes before you start. Every shift includes a thirty-minute break, and before anyone asks, yes, you're paid for it.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: A few of you have asked about night shifts. There's no extra pay for those, I'm afraid, but you do get the following day off. And the rota is drawn up by my team, so you can't pick your own shifts online, although you can ask to change them, which I'll come back to.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Now, rules. Some of them might surprise you. Phones, for instance: we'd actually like you to keep them switched on, because we send updates to a staff group chat. And photos are fine anywhere, even backstage, as long as you don't post the backstage ones online.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: But there are two rules we're very strict about. You mustn't drink alcohol while you're wearing your staff T-shirt, even after your shift if you haven't changed. And your wristband is for you alone, so no bringing friends or family onto the site, not even for half an hour. Oh, and footwear: trainers are fine, you don't need safety boots, just nothing open-toed.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Right, the last thing, and probably the most important, is who to contact. You'll get a card with all the numbers on, but let me go through it. If you need to change a shift, say you've swapped with a friend, you might think your area supervisor can sort it out, but they can't. That has to go through the staff office, which is the green cabin behind the main stage.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: If your wristband gets damaged, or you lose it, go to the accreditation desk at the staff entrance. They'll print you a new one, but it costs £15, so do look after it.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Next, unattended bags. Please don't pick them up and carry them over to lost property, and don't open them. Just radio security control and stay nearby until someone arrives.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Something that happens every year is a child who's lost their parents. Your first thought might be to call security, or to take them to the medical centre, but neither is right unless the child's hurt. Walk them to the information point by the main gate, because that's where our welfare team is based.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: If there's a problem with your meal vouchers, so you haven't been given any, or a food stall won't accept them, speak to the catering manager. Each voucher's worth £8, by the way, and you get two per shift. And if you're running late, don't ring the staff office, because they won't pass the message on in time. Call your area supervisor directly, since they're the one who'll need to find cover.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Finally, if you hurt yourself while you're working, even if it's only a small cut, you must go to the medical centre so it's recorded. Don't just ask a colleague for a plaster. Oh, and if you miss the last staff shuttle bus back to town, the transport desk closes at midnight, so plan ahead. Right, any questions before we hand out the T-shirts?
turns.speaker: manager

parts.title: Planning a food waste project

turns.text: Okay, Tyler, we need to get our plan for the food waste project to Professor Haddad by Friday. Shall we start with why we picked the topic? She wants that in the introduction.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure. I mean, there were some good ideas on her list of suggested topics, like the one on coffee cup packaging, but we didn't go with any of those.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. It really came from you, didn't it? From your job.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah. When I was working shifts at a campus cafe last semester, I couldn't believe how much went in the trash at closing. Whole trays of muffins and sandwiches. That's what got me thinking about it.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. And it's not as if the data's easy to get, so we can't say we chose it because it was convenient.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Ha, no, definitely not.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, next, which cafe. I know we talked about the student union one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Well, it's the busiest, so it would have been ideal, but the manager there turned us down. Too busy, she said.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: What about the little place in the science building?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I looked into that, but it only sells coffee and a few snacks. There just wouldn't be enough waste to measure. So the library cafe is really our best option, and the manager there's already said yes.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Great, the library one it is. Now, how do we actually measure the waste? My first thought was just counting the items left unsold at the end of the day.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That would be quicker, but it misses everything people leave on their plates. Half-eaten sandwiches, that kind of thing.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. And I don't think taking photos of the trays would give us real numbers either.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. So I think we should weigh it. Everything that's thrown away, unsold or not, goes on a scale.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, weighing it is. That'll be messy, but fine.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: We also wanted a short survey for customers, right? About why they leave food.

parts.title: Glaciers as stores of fresh water

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Hamish Calloway, and today we're continuing our unit on the water cycle by looking at glaciers, which, as you'll see, are enormous stores of fresh water. I'll start with how they form, then look at how they release water to rivers and farms, and I'll finish with what happens when they shrink.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, so how does a glacier form? Lots of places get heavy snow in winter, but that alone isn't enough. For a glacier to develop, the snow has to survive the summer, so that some of it's still lying there when the next winter's snow arrives. Then it builds up, layer on layer, year after year.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: As those layers get thicker, something interesting happens underneath. The weight of the new snow presses down on the older snow, and the grains get packed closer and closer together. Over time the air between the grains is squeezed out, and what you end up with is dense, solid ice. In very cold places, that can take well over a century.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: If you've been up to Franz Josef or Fox Glacier on the West Coast, you'll have noticed that the ice often looks blue. A lot of people assume it's reflecting the sky, but that's not it. Because the ice is so dense, it absorbs the red part of sunlight, and the blue light is what's left for us to see.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so how much water are we actually talking about? You'll sometimes see three-quarters quoted, but the more accurate figure is that glaciers and ice sheets hold about 70 per cent of the world's fresh water. Now, most of that isn't in places like New Zealand, or even Iceland. It's locked up in two huge ice sheets: the one covering Antarctica, which is by far the largest, and the one on Greenland.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But it's the smaller mountain glaciers that matter most for people, because that's the water that ends up in rivers. Some researchers call them batteries, but the term you'll see most often in the literature is water towers. The idea is that they store water high up in the mountains and let it out gradually.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And the timing of that release is the key point. Snow and ice melt fastest in the hottest months, which tends to be exactly when there's the least rain. So glacier meltwater keeps rivers flowing during droughts, when they might otherwise drop very low or even dry up completely.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: You may also have noticed that glacial rivers are a strange milky, turquoise colour. That's caused by tiny particles of rock which the glacier grinds up as it moves over the ground. It's sometimes loosely described as silt, but geologists call this glacial flour, and it's so fine that it stays in the water for a long way downstream.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, let's think about who uses this water. Here in Canterbury, rivers fed partly by snow and ice from the Southern Alps, the Rakaia, for example, supply irrigation schemes right across the plains. Traditionally that land was mostly used for sheep, but these days a large share of the irrigation water goes to dairy farms, which need pasture to keep growing right through summer.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And it's the same story, on a much bigger scale, in other parts of the world. In Central Asia, for example, rivers that start in the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains water huge areas of farmland. Some wheat is grown there, and some rice, but the crop that depends most heavily on meltwater is cotton, which needs a great deal of water in the dry growing season.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, so finally, what happens as glaciers shrink? Almost all mountain glaciers are getting smaller, and New Zealand's have lost a large share of their ice since the late 1960s, sorry, the late 1970s, when regular surveys began. Now, you might expect river flow to drop straight away. But a glacier that's losing ice faster than it gains it actually releases extra water, so at first, flows increase.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Eventually, though, the glacier gets so small that the amount of melt starts to fall. The point where meltwater reaches its maximum is called peak water, and after that, rivers get less every year. For many rivers in Asia and South America, scientists think that point has already passed, or will within the next twenty years or so.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There's a second danger as well. As glaciers retreat, they often leave behind lakes held back only by piles of loose rock that the ice pushed up. If one of those natural dams gives way, the water can empty out in minutes and cause sudden, destructive floods in the valleys below.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, to sum up, glaciers aren't just beautiful scenery. They're a kind of savings account of water that many communities have been drawing on, and once it's spent, it isn't easily replaced. Next week we'll look at groundwater, which raises some similar questions. Okay, any questions before we finish?
turns.speaker: lecturer

parts.title: A new bike-share program

turns.text: Good morning, and thanks for having me on the show. I'm Erin Castellano from the City of Riverton's transportation office. You've probably noticed the bright green bikes all over downtown lately. That's Ride Riverton, our new bike-share program, and it's been running for just over six weeks.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: So, why did we set it up? A lot of people assume it's mainly for tourists, and sure, visitors do use it. It might also take a few cars off the road downtown, which would be great. But the main reason was commuters: too many people were getting off the train at Union Station with no easy way to cover the last mile to their offices.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Now, how do you get started? Originally, the idea was that you'd pick up a membership card at the public library, but we dropped that because it added an extra step. There's also a Ride Riverton app, which plenty of people like, but you don't have to download it. All you do is walk up to the screen at any station, tap your bank card, and sign up right there.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Right, let's talk money, because that's what everyone asks me about. When the program was first announced, we said a single ride would cost $3.50. But the city council voted to bring that down to $2.75 for the first year, to encourage people to try it. That covers thirty minutes, and if you go over, it's an extra $1.50 for each additional half hour.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: If you ride regularly, an annual pass is better value at $90 a year. We did look at a discount for students, but the colleges here already pay for their students' transit passes. A reduced rate for seniors is something we're still discussing. What we have done is cut the annual pass in half for anyone who holds the city's low-income transit card.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Okay, where are the bikes? Right now there are twenty-two stations. You'd probably expect the biggest one to be at Union Station, and it's busy, with thirty docks. But the largest is actually down at Harbor Park on the waterfront, which has forty-five, because weekend demand there is huge. There's also a smaller one outside the central library.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Now, what if you arrive at a station and every dock is full? Please don't just lock the bike to a fence or a lamppost, because you'll be charged a fee. And you don't need to call us, either. Just tap the screen at the full station, and it'll give you fifteen extra minutes free to ride to the nearest one with space.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: So, how has it gone so far? Really well overall, with over forty thousand rides. We expected complaints about the seats, but they adjust easily and hardly anyone's mentioned them. The app did crash briefly on the first day, sorry, the first morning, but that was fixed within hours. What people actually complained about most was that early in the morning, stations in residential neighborhoods were often empty.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: That happens because everyone rides downtown in the morning and the bikes stay there. Some people suggested charging more during the morning rush, but we don't want to punish commuters. And adding extra docks wouldn't help much if the stations are empty anyway.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: So we've got two fixes. Starting next week, vans will collect bikes from downtown overnight and bring them back out to the neighborhoods. And then, to encourage riders to help us out, there's a new reward system: if you finish a ride at one of the stations marked in blue on the app, you'll get ride credit added to your account.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Looking ahead, we've got some bigger changes coming this summer. At the moment, the bikes are locked between midnight and 5 a.m., but from June first they'll be available around the clock. Lots of parents have asked us for child seats, but for safety reasons we've decided not to offer them. We're also adding a hundred electric bikes in June, which should really help with the hills on the north side. Stations east of the river are definitely coming too, but not until next spring, I'm afraid.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Finally, we'd love your ideas on where new stations should go. Please don't email suggestions, because honestly, they're hard for us to keep track of. Instead, go to our website and drop a pin on the interactive map. Our online survey closed back in March, but if you'd rather talk to us in person, there's an open public meeting at the Eastside Community Center on May 14th at 7 p.m.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Bring your questions and your ideas. Thanks so much for listening, and I'll see you out on the bikes!
turns.speaker: officer

parts.title: Railways and the growth of towns: essay feedback

turns.text: Come in, Tom, have a seat. So, I've read the draft of your essay on early railways and the growth of towns, and overall it's a promising piece of work.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Oh, that's a relief. I wasn't sure the argument really came across.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: It mostly does. You're claiming that the railways didn't just speed up growth, they actually decided which towns grew at all. That's a bold claim, so your sources really matter. Shall we go through them one by one?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Yes, please.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Let's start with the railway company timetables. You've used them to show how often trains stopped at each town.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: I was a bit worried about those, to be honest. They're rather dry.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Dry, perhaps, but they're actually the most convincing material you've got. They're hard facts about which towns were connected and when, so I'd keep them right at the centre of the essay.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Great. And the census returns? I put loads of figures from those in the middle sections.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: The figures themselves are fine, they're accurate. The trouble is that whole pages of numbers interrupt your argument. Take the full tables out of the main text and put them at the back, after the conclusion. Then just mention the key figures in your paragraphs.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: OK. What about the newspaper reports? I quoted the Midland Courier quite a lot.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Yes, and you need to remember who owned that paper. Several of its directors had shares in the railway company, so naturally it praised every new line. You don't have to drop it, but you should point out that it may not give a balanced picture.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: I hadn't thought of that. Then there's the travel diary, the one written by the engineer's wife.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: That's a lovely find. I'm not worried about bias there, actually, because she's quite critical of the railway in places. But you've copied out long passages, sometimes half a page at a time. A sentence or two would make the point.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Right, I'll trim those. And the town council minutes?
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Those are useful, but you've only said they're from the 1840s, without saying which meeting. The reader needs to know exactly when each decision was taken, because timing is central to your argument. Did the council plan the new streets before or after the station opened?
turns.speaker: tutor

parts.title: Restoring damaged coral reefs

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Last week we looked at how coral reefs form, so today I'd like to turn to something a bit more hopeful: how scientists are trying to repair reefs that have already been damaged. I'll start with why reefs decline, then talk about coral gardening, then some newer methods, and I'll finish with how we actually measure success.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. The biggest threat by far is bleaching. Corals have tiny algae living inside their tissue, and most people think of these algae as the thing that gives coral its colour. That's true, but more importantly, they produce the bulk of the coral's food, something like ninety per cent of it. So when the water gets too warm and the coral pushes the algae out, it turns white and basically starts to starve.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second threat is the crown-of-thorns starfish. Despite the dramatic name, it's simply a starfish that feeds on coral, and normally there aren't many of them around. But fertiliser washing off farms and down the rivers here in Queensland seems to help their young survive. So every few years we get huge outbreaks, and they can strip a section of reef in a matter of months.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then there are cyclones. A severe cyclone doesn't just damage individual corals; it can smash the whole structure into loose rubble. And that's a real headache, because rubble rolls around with every wave, so any baby coral that settles on it gets crushed or buried. Some sites can stay bare for decades because of that.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK, so what can we do about it? The best-known approach is coral gardening. Divers collect small fragments from healthy corals and grow them in an underwater nursery. The first nurseries were basically flat tables sitting on the seabed, but these days most teams use frames that look rather like trees, with branches made of plastic pipe, and the fragments hang from those branches in the open water.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: How long do they stay in the nursery? Students often guess a few weeks, but it's a good deal longer than that. Fast-growing species might be ready in six months, but on average it's around nine months before the fragments are big enough to go back onto the reef. Then divers attach them to the reef one by one, usually with a kind of underwater cement.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, coral gardening is sometimes criticised for being expensive. Actually, the costs have come down a lot in the last ten years. The real weakness is that it's slow. A good team might plant a few thousand corals in a season, but when you remember that the Great Barrier Reef covers an area bigger than Italy, you can see the problem.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And that brings me to some newer methods. One is sometimes called coral IVF. Many corals reproduce in a mass spawning event, which happens just once a year, usually a few nights after a full moon in late spring. Researchers head out after dark and collect the eggs and sperm floating on the surface.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: They raise the larvae in floating pools for about a week, sorry, five days, and then release them over a damaged patch of reef. The tricky part is that larvae drift away very easily. So the team covers the area with what they call a mesh tent, which keeps the larvae in place for several days while they settle.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Another line of research is breeding tougher corals. A few years ago some labs were looking at corals that could resist pollution, but the main focus now is heat. The idea is to cross corals that came through a bad bleaching year, in the hope that their offspring will cope better with warmer water.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And here's one I really like. A reef isn't only coral; it needs fish, which graze on the seaweed and keep the coral clear. Healthy reefs are surprisingly noisy, with shrimps crackling and fish grunting. Researchers found that if you put underwater speakers on a damaged reef and play recordings of a healthy one, young fish are drawn to it, and a lot of them stay.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, how do we know if any of this actually works? That's a question people in the field have argued about for years. For a long time, projects simply reported the number of corals they'd planted. It makes a nice headline, but it tells you very little, because many of those corals might be dead a year later. So now we look at survival rates and at how much of the seabed is covered by living coral.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But for me, the real test comes later. Growing bigger is good, and getting through a hot summer is even better. A restored reef is only truly successful when the corals we've put out there begin to reproduce on their own, because then the reef can start rebuilding itself without our help.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, that's all for today. For next week, please read the chapter on reef monitoring, and have a look at the photos from our own nursery off Heron Island, which I've put online.
turns.speaker: lecturer

questions.prompt: Why reefs decline: algae living inside corals produce around 90% of their ______
questions.evidence: they produce the bulk of the coral's food, something like ninety per cent of it

explanation.en: The lecturer says the algae give coral its colour, but more importantly they make about ninety per cent of its food. Colour does not fit '90%'.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что водоросли придают кораллу цвет, но, что важнее, они дают около девяноста процентов его пищи («food»). Цвет («colour») не подходит к «90%».
explanation.uk: Лекторка каже, що водорості надають коралу кольору, але, що важливіше, вони дають близько дев'яноста відсотків його їжі («food»). Колір («colour») не підходить до «90%».

questions.prompt: Fertiliser from farms is linked to outbreaks of coral-eating ______
questions.evidence: it's simply a starfish that feeds on coral

explanation.en: The crown-of-thorns starfish eats coral, and fertiliser in rivers helps its young survive, causing outbreaks.
explanation.ru: Морская звезда «crown-of-thorns starfish» питается кораллами, а удобрения («fertiliser»), попадающие в реки, помогают выживать её молоди. Из-за этого происходят вспышки её численности.
explanation.uk: Морська зірка «crown-of-thorns starfish» живиться коралами, а добрива («fertiliser»), що потрапляють у річки, допомагають виживати її молоді. Через це стаються спалахи її чисельності.

questions.prompt: Cyclones can break reefs into loose ______, where young corals get crushed
questions.evidence: it can smash the whole structure into loose rubble

explanation.en: Severe cyclones smash the reef into rubble, which moves with the waves and crushes or buries baby corals.
explanation.ru: Сильные циклоны («cyclones») разбивают риф на обломки («rubble»). Волны носят эти обломки, и они давят или засыпают молодые кораллы.
explanation.uk: Потужні циклони («cyclones») розбивають риф на уламки («rubble»). Хвилі носять ці уламки, і вони розчавлюють або засипають молоді корали.

questions.prompt: Coral gardening: most nurseries now use frames that resemble ______
questions.evidence: most teams use frames that look rather like trees

explanation.en: The first nurseries used flat tables, but today most use frames that look like trees, so 'tables' is wrong.
explanation.ru: В первых питомниках использовали плоские столы, но сегодня в большинстве из них стоят каркасы, похожие на деревья («trees»), поэтому «tables» — неверный ответ.
explanation.uk: У перших розсадниках використовували пласкі столи, але сьогодні в більшості з них стоять каркаси, схожі на дерева («trees»), тому «tables» — неправильна відповідь.

questions.prompt: Fragments usually grow for about ______ months before planting
questions.evidence: on average it's around nine months

explanation.en: Six months is only for fast-growing species; the average time is about nine months.
explanation.ru: Шесть месяцев («six months») — это срок только для быстрорастущих видов, а в среднем на это уходит около девяти месяцев («nine»).
explanation.uk: Шість місяців («six months») — це термін лише для видів, що швидко ростуть, а в середньому на це йде близько дев'яти місяців («nine»).

questions.prompt: Main weakness: the method is too ______ for very large reefs
questions.evidence: The real weakness is that it's slow.

explanation.en: People criticise the cost, but the lecturer says costs have fallen; the real problem is that it is slow.
explanation.ru: Метод часто критикуют за стоимость («cost»), но лектор говорит, что затраты снизились. Настоящая проблема в том, что он медленный («slow»).
explanation.uk: Метод часто критикують за вартість («cost»), але лекторка каже, що витрати знизилися. Справжня проблема в тому, що він повільний («slow»).

questions.prompt: New methods: mass spawning occurs a few nights after a full ______
questions.evidence: usually a few nights after a full moon in late spring

explanation.en: Mass spawning happens once a year, a few nights after a full moon.
explanation.ru: Массовый нерест происходит раз в год, через несколько ночей после полнолуния («full moon»).
explanation.uk: Масовий нерест відбувається раз на рік, через кілька ночей після повного місяця («full moon»).

questions.prompt: Larvae are held on the damaged reef under a mesh ______
questions.evidence: covers the area with what they call a mesh tent

explanation.en: The larvae are first raised in floating pools, but on the reef they are kept in place by a mesh tent.
explanation.ru: Сначала личинок выращивают в плавучих бассейнах («pools»), но на рифе их удерживает на месте сетчатый тент («mesh tent»).
explanation.uk: Спочатку личинок вирощують у плавучих басейнах («pools»), але на рифі їх утримує на місці сітчастий намет («mesh tent»).

questions.prompt: Breeding programmes mainly aim to produce corals that can tolerate ______
questions.evidence: but the main focus now is heat

explanation.en: Some labs once studied resistance to pollution, but the main focus today is coping with heat.
explanation.ru: Некоторые лаборатории раньше изучали устойчивость к загрязнению («pollution»), но сегодня главное направление — то, как кораллы справляются с жарой («heat»).
explanation.uk: Деякі лабораторії раніше вивчали стійкість до забруднення («pollution»), але сьогодні головний напрям — те, як корали витримують спеку («heat»).

questions.prompt: Recordings of a healthy reef played through speakers attract young ______
questions.evidence: young fish are drawn to it, and a lot of them stay

explanation.en: Shrimps are part of the noise on the recordings, but it is young fish that are attracted to the reef.
explanation.ru: Креветки («shrimps») тоже создают часть шума на записях, но к рифу привлекают именно молодых рыб («fish»).
explanation.uk: Креветки («shrimps») теж створюють частину шуму на записах, але до рифу приваблюють саме молодих риб («fish»).

parts.title: Reporting a lost bag

turns.text: Good morning, Lakeside Transit lost and found. This is Ray Donnelly speaking. How can I help you?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Hi, yes. I left my bag on one of your buses this week, and I'm really hoping somebody handed it in. I've already looked everywhere at home, just in case.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Okay, let's see what we can do. I'll start a report for you first. Can I get your name, please?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Sure. It's Paula Kessler.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Is that K-E-S-L-E-R?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Almost. There are two S's. Kessler, K-E-S-S-L-E-R.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Got it, thanks. And which bus were you on?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: It was the number 74. Oh, wait, no, sorry. The 74 is the one I take home. I was on the 47, the one that runs downtown.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The 47, okay. And what day was that?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: I was going to say Monday, because I had a dentist appointment that day, but they moved it. So it was Tuesday, around four in the afternoon.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Tuesday, around four. Do you remember where you got off?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Yes, I got on at Main Street and got off at the stop on Carlton Avenue, right by the hospital. That's C-A-R-L-T-O-N.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Great. Now, can you describe the bag for me?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: It's a backpack, medium size. It looks kind of gray in some light, but it's actually dark green.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Dark green. And what's it made of? Is it leather, or nylon, or something else?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Not leather, no. It's canvas, the thick kind. It's a little worn at the bottom.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Is there anything that would help us recognize it? We get a lot of backpacks in here, and many of them look the same.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Well, there used to be a keychain on the zipper, but that fell off months ago. Oh, but there's a flag sewn onto the front pocket. A small Canadian one. My sister brought it back from Toronto.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's really helpful. Okay, and what was inside the bag?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Let me think. A water bottle, a couple of magazines, some snacks. My wallet isn't in there, thank goodness. I keep that in my coat. But my camera is, and that's what I'm really worried about. It was a birthday present.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: I understand. We'll do our best. Now, what's the best number to reach you on?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: My home number is 773 555 0129, but honestly, I'm hardly ever there. You'd better call my cell. That's 773 555 0186.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Let me read that back. 773 555 0186.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: That's right.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Okay. I've checked our system, and nothing matching your bag has been logged yet. But items from the buses don't always reach us right away. Sometimes it takes two or three days, so please don't worry yet.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Oh, okay. And how long do you hold on to things?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We used to keep everything for 60 days, but the policy changed last year. Now it's 30 days. After that, items go to charity.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Okay. Is there a charge for that?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: If you pick it up yourself, there's a handling fee of $5. We can also send it to your home, but that costs $12, because of the delivery.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Oh, I'll just come in. It's not far from my office.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Sounds good. As soon as your bag shows up, we'll give you a call on your cell.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Thank you so much. You've been really helpful.
turns.speaker: caller

parts.title: Welcome to Wattle Creek Wildlife Sanctuary

turns.text: G'day, everyone, and welcome to Wattle Creek Wildlife Sanctuary. My name's Brett Kinsella, and I'm one of the guides here. Before you head off, I'll give you a quick idea of where everything is, and then I'll run through today's talks and feeding times. So grab one of our maps and have it handy.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right. So you've just come in through the main gate, and you're at the bottom of the main path, which runs north through the middle of the sanctuary. On your left is the Visitor Centre, where you bought your tickets, and that's also where you'll find the toilets and the gift shop. A lot of people go looking for food in there, but the café's actually directly across from it, on the right-hand side of the path as you come in. It does good coffee, and the sausage rolls are excellent.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, now walk north up the main path. Just past the Visitor Centre, there's another building on your left, right on the corner where our two paths cross. That's the reptile house. It's air-conditioned, so it's a good place to cool down if it gets hot this arvo.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Keep going straight over the crossroads and right to the end of the main path, and that's where you'll find the koalas. You'll notice the eucalyptus grove up in the north-west corner, and some visitors expect to see koalas in there. But that's just where we grow the leaves we feed them, so don't waste your time looking up in those trees.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, come back down to the crossroads and turn right, so you're heading east along the cross path. The first building on your left is the aviary, with our parrots and cockatoos. Behind it, further north, there's a smaller building, and that's the nocturnal house, where you can see bilbies and possums. It's kept dark inside, so give your eyes a minute to adjust.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: On the opposite side of the cross path, the south side, there's a grassy area right on the corner of the main path, with the lake just to the east of it. That's the picnic area. There are tables and barbecues, and you're welcome to bring your own lunch. Just keep an eye on your sandwiches, because the ducks from the lake are very bold.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, last bit of the map. Go back to the crossroads and this time head west, past the reptile house. Right at the far end of the path, on your left, you'll find the wombat burrows. They dig all day, so you might only see the tops of their heads.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, on the other side of the path, opposite the wombats, there's a big open field, just south of the eucalyptus grove. That's the kangaroo paddock, and you're allowed to walk right in among them. They're very relaxed.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, now for today's programme. The koala talk is usually at 11 o'clock, but today it's been pushed back half an hour, to 11:30, because the keeper's had to take one of the joeys to the vet. Nothing serious, I'm told. It runs for about thirty minutes, so you'll be finished by 12, in time for lunch.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: At one o'clock there's the reptile talk, in the reptile house. Visitors used to be able to hold one of our pythons, but we stopped that last year, sorry. What you can do is give one of our blue-tongue lizards a gentle stroke. People sometimes ask about feeding the turtles too, but only the keepers are allowed to do that.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Then at two o'clock, sorry, quarter past two, the keepers feed the kangaroos, and you can join in. Please don't give them bread or anything you've brought from home, because it makes them sick. You'll need one of our special feed bags, which are $3 each from the Visitor Centre. Not the café, by the way. They don't sell them there.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Normally at three o'clock we'd have the free-flight bird show near the aviary, but I'm afraid it's off today. It's a bit windy, but that's not the reason, the birds are fine with a breeze, and they're all perfectly healthy. It's because workers are fixing the aviary roof this afternoon, and the noise would upset them.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Finally, the wombat feeding is at quarter to four, at the burrows. There's no seating there, so it's standing room only, and please, no flash photography, as it frightens them. My advice is to get there about ten minutes before it starts, because the viewing area fills up quickly.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, that's it from me. If you've got any questions, just look for me or any of the staff in green shirts. Enjoy your day!
turns.speaker: guide

explanation.ru: Если идти на запад мимо террариума, норы вомбатов — в дальнем конце дорожки слева (с южной стороны).
explanation.uk: Якщо йти на захід повз тераріум, нори вомбатів — у дальньому кінці доріжки ліворуч (з південного боку).

segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students planning a presentation about sleep and how it affects students' exam results. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
