parts.title: Sleep and exam performance

turns.text: Okay, Holly, shall we get going on this presentation? We've got fifteen minutes on sleep and exam performance, and we need to send the tutor an outline by Friday.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yeah, sounds good. Before we get into the individual studies, though, can I just say what surprised me in the background reading? I'd assumed students would have a fair idea of how much they sleep, but apparently most of them reckon they get far more than they really do.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Mm, I noticed that too. And I'd always been told naps were a bad idea, that they ruin your sleep at night.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Same here, but the reading said a short nap's fine, and that didn't really surprise me, because my flatmate swears by them. No, the thing that got me was how long one bad night lasts. You miss a single night's sleep and your memory still isn't back to normal three days later.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, that's quite something. I wasn't surprised that nearly all the research was done on university students rather than school kids, though. I suppose they're easy to recruit.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. And did anything about the research itself bother you?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Well, a lot of it depends on students saying how long they slept. Nobody actually measured it. They just filled in a questionnaire afterwards.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right, and given what we just said about people overestimating, that's a real weakness. I thought the samples might be tiny too, but most had several hundred participants, so that's fine.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And they're mostly from the last ten years, so they're not out of date.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. But what none of them seemed to ask about was paid work. Heaps of students do evening shifts in cafés or bars, and that's bound to affect both their sleep and their marks.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Good point, we should mention that. So, how do we actually present all this? I found a documentary clip that might work as an opener.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: How long is it?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Twelve minutes. Ah, right, that's most of our slot.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Exactly. What if we kick off by asking everyone how many hours they slept last night? Just a show of hands. It gets them involved straight away.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I like that. We could also run a quick memory test with the audience, you know, read out a list of words.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, I think that's risky. It might not work with a tired class at nine in the morning. Let's keep it simple.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. Should we split the speaking fifty-fifty?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I'd rather you took the studies, since you've read more of them, and I'll do the intro and conclusion. It won't be exactly even, but that's okay. Oh, and let's give everyone a one-page summary sheet with the references on it, so the slides aren't crammed.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great. Right, the studies themselves. Let's go through them and check we agree on what each one found. First, the Auckland study of first-year students.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's the one comparing students who went to bed around the same time every night with those whose bedtimes were all over the place. The regular group ended up with better marks, even though the total hours they slept were about the same.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Then there's the study of trainee nurses. They were tested after a night shift. Their memory for patient details was actually fine, but they made far more mistakes when working out drug doses.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Which is a bit scary. The German lab study's next. Half the participants had a ninety-minute nap after learning some word lists, and the others stayed awake.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And, interestingly, both groups remembered about the same number of words, but the nap group were much quicker at spotting a hidden rule in a puzzle afterwards.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay. Then the big American online survey, over two thousand students. That's the odd one out, because it found that how long people slept made no difference to their grades at all.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Though again, that's all self-reported, so we can point that out. What about the Wellington study? That was secondary school pupils, wasn't it?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yes. They asked about sport and exercise, but that showed nothing much. What did stand out was that pupils who were on their phones after eleven at night got about forty minutes less sleep.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. And the Japanese one looked at students who lost sleep during the week and then slept in on Saturday and Sunday. They still did worse in Monday's tests, so the extra hours didn't make up for it.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I'd actually hoped one of these would test all-night revision directly, but none of them did. Anyway, last is the Australian study where students kept sleep diaries.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Mm, and what predicted their marks wasn't how long they spent in bed, it was how often they woke up during the night.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, so that gives us a nice range. Let's write the outline tonight.
turns.speaker: student_a

options.text: short naps disturbing students' sleep at night
memory problems lasting days after one lost night
students believing they sleep more than they do
students today sleeping less than in the past
most studies being done with university students

questions.prompt: Which TWO things surprised Holly in the background reading?
questions.evidence: most of them reckon they get far more than they really do

explanation.en: Holly is surprised that students think they sleep much more than they actually do, and that memory is still affected three days after one sleepless night. The reading said short naps are fine, and it is Sam, not Holly, who mentions the research being on university students, and he was not surprised.
explanation.ru: Holly удивлена тем, что студенты думают, будто спят намного больше, чем на самом деле, и что память всё ещё страдает через три дня после одной бессонной ночи. В прочитанном тексте говорилось, что короткий дневной сон не вредит. А о том, что исследование проводилось на студентах университета, говорит Sam, а не Holly, и его это не удивило.
explanation.uk: Holly здивована тим, що студенти думають, ніби сплять набагато більше, ніж насправді, і що пам'ять досі страждає через три дні після однієї безсонної ночі. У прочитаному тексті йшлося про те, що короткий денний сон не шкодить. А про те, що дослідження проводили на студентах університету, згадує Sam, а не Holly, і його це не здивувало.

questions.prompt: The Auckland study of first-year students
questions.evidence: The regular group ended up with better marks, even though the total hours they slept were about the same.

explanation.en: Students who went to bed at about the same time every night got better marks. The number of hours was similar, so the key factor was the regular bedtime.
explanation.ru: Студенты, которые каждый вечер ложились спать примерно в одно и то же время, получали более высокие оценки. Количество часов сна было примерно одинаковым, поэтому главным фактором было именно регулярное время отхода ко сну.
explanation.uk: Студенти, які щовечора лягали спати приблизно в один і той самий час, отримували вищі оцінки. Кількість годин сну була приблизно однаковою, тож ключовим чинником був саме регулярний час відходу до сну.

questions.prompt: The study of trainee nurses
questions.evidence: they made far more mistakes when working out drug doses

explanation.en: After a night shift the nurses made more mistakes calculating drug doses. Their memory for patient details was fine, so it was not about recall.
explanation.ru: После ночной смены медсёстры чаще ошибались при расчёте доз лекарств. С памятью на данные пациентов всё было в порядке, так что дело было не в запоминании.
explanation.uk: Після нічної зміни медсестри частіше помилялися, розраховуючи дози ліків. З пам'яттю на дані пацієнтів усе було гаразд, тож річ була не в запам'ятовуванні.

questions.prompt: The German laboratory study
questions.evidence: the nap group were much quicker at spotting a hidden rule in a puzzle afterwards

explanation.en: The group who napped solved a puzzle faster. Both groups remembered the same number of words, so the finding was about problem-solving, not memory.
explanation.ru: Группа, которая поспала днём, быстрее решила головоломку. Обе группы запомнили одинаковое количество слов, так что результат касался решения задач, а не памяти.
explanation.uk: Група, яка поспала вдень, швидше розв'язала головоломку. Обидві групи запам'ятали однакову кількість слів, тож результат стосувався розв'язання задач, а не пам'яті.

questions.prompt: The American online survey
questions.evidence: how long people slept made no difference to their grades at all

explanation.en: This survey found that the amount of sleep did not affect grades, which is why Holly calls it the odd one out.
explanation.ru: Этот опрос показал, что количество сна не влияло на оценки, поэтому Holly называет его "the odd one out" — исключением из общего ряда.
explanation.uk: Це опитування показало, що кількість сну не впливала на оцінки, тому Holly називає його "the odd one out" — винятком із загального ряду.

questions.prompt: The Wellington study of secondary school pupils
questions.evidence: pupils who were on their phones after eleven at night got about forty minutes less sleep

explanation.en: Using phones late at night meant pupils slept about forty minutes less. The study also asked about exercise, but that showed nothing much.
explanation.ru: Из-за того, что школьники пользовались телефонами поздно вечером, они спали примерно на сорок минут меньше. В исследовании также спрашивали о физических нагрузках, но это почти ничего не показало.
explanation.uk: Через те, що школярі користувалися телефонами пізно ввечері, вони спали приблизно на сорок хвилин менше. У дослідженні також питали про фізичні навантаження, але це майже нічого не показало.

questions.prompt: The Japanese study
questions.evidence: They still did worse in Monday's tests, so the extra hours didn't make up for it.

explanation.en: Students who slept in at the weekend after losing sleep during the week still did worse, so the extra weekend sleep did not repair the loss.
explanation.ru: Студенты, которые отсыпались в выходные после недосыпа в течение недели, всё равно учились хуже, так что дополнительный сон в выходные не восполнял потерю.
explanation.uk: Студенти, які відсипалися на вихідних після недосипання протягом тижня, все одно навчалися гірше, тож додатковий сон на вихідних не компенсував втрати.

parts.title: The history of papermaking

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Dr Edward Lockwood, and today we're continuing our series on everyday technologies with something you probably take for granted: paper. I'll begin with how it was first made, then look at how the craft spread westwards, and I'll finish with the machines of the nineteenth century and recycling today.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. Before paper, people wrote on all sorts of surfaces. The Egyptians used papyrus, which is where our word 'paper' comes from, and in China people wrote on strips of bamboo or on silk. The trouble was that bamboo was heavy and silk was very expensive, so there was a real need for something better.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The traditional date for the invention of paper is the year 105, when a court official called Cai Lun presented the process to the emperor. Archaeologists have since found older fragments, so he probably improved the method rather than inventing it. Let's go through the process step by step, as it was carried out in his time.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: First, the raw materials were collected: the inner bark of the mulberry tree, hemp, old rags and even worn-out fishing nets. These were chopped into small pieces and left to soak in water. Now, you might expect salt to be added at this point, but in fact what they added was lime, which helped to break the material down.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Next, the softened material was beaten with wooden hammers. This was hard, tiring work, and it could go on for hours, until the fibres separated and formed a thick pulp. That was mixed with plenty of water in a large vat. Then came the clever part. The papermaker dipped a screen into the vat and lifted it out, covered in a thin layer of fibres. The earliest screens were made of cloth, but cloth tended to sag, so they soon switched to bamboo, which kept the sheet perfectly flat.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The water drained away through the screen, and the wet sheet was pressed to squeeze out the rest. Some workshops hung their sheets on lines, rather like washing, but the usual method was to brush each one onto a heated wall, where it dried in just a few minutes. And the last stage? Once it was completely dry, the sheet was polished with a smooth stone, so that ink wouldn't spread across it. Some makers tried shells for this, but stone gave a better finish.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK, so how did this knowledge leave China? For several centuries it was kept fairly secret. The usual story is that it reached Samarkand, in Central Asia, in 751, after a battle in which Chinese papermakers were taken prisoner. Samarkand had clean rivers, but plenty of towns had those. What really made it successful was the flax grown all around the city, which gave a steady supply of fibre.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: From there, the craft moved to Baghdad, where a paper mill was working by the 790s. Government offices were quick to adopt it. Until then, official records had been kept on parchment, made from animal skin, and paper replaced it partly because it was cheaper, but mainly because anything scraped off paper left a visible mark, so documents were much harder to forge.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Papermaking then crossed North Africa and reached Spain in the twelfth century, and Italy shortly afterwards. The Italian mills, especially in a town called Fabriano, made several improvements. They used animal glue to give the paper a harder surface, which is interesting, but the innovation I'd like you to note down is the watermark. These were faint designs pressed into each sheet, so that buyers could tell which mill had produced it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, let's jump to the nineteenth century. By around 1800, demand was growing fast because of newspapers and the spread of schooling, but European paper was still made from rags, and there simply weren't enough of them to go round. Some mills even put up notices asking households to save their old clothes.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Hand production was also slow. A skilled team might manage a few thousand sheets a day. The answer was the machine developed in England by the Fourdrinier brothers and patented in 1806. Instead of producing separate sheets, it made paper as one continuous roll, which could then be cut to whatever size the customer wanted.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: That still left the problem of raw materials. From the 1840s, the solution was wood pulp, which was cheap and almost unlimited. But this new paper had a serious flaw. It contained acid from the production process, and over time that acid makes paper turn yellow and brittle. British libraries now spend millions of pounds trying to rescue books from this period, while much older rag paper is often in far better condition.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, recycling. A lot of people believe paper can be recycled forever, but it can't. Each time it goes through the process, the fibres get shorter and weaker. You'll see figures of five times quoted, but most experts put the limit at around seven, after which the fibres are too short to bond together.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: People also worry about ink, but that's actually removed quite easily, using soap and air bubbles that carry it to the surface. The real headache for recycling plants is grease from things like takeaway pizza boxes, because it can't be separated from the fibres, and it ruins a whole batch. Next week, we'll look at printing.
turns.speaker: lecturer

explanation.uk: Папір досі робили з "rags", а їх не вистачало, щоб задовольнити зростаючий попит.

explanation.uk: Замість окремих аркушів машина робила один безперервний рулон ("roll"), який можна було розрізати на аркуші будь-якого розміру.

parts.title: Booking a holiday sports camp

turns.text: Good morning, Riverside Holiday Sports Camp, Alison Pritchard speaking. How can I help?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about your summer camp. My daughter's really keen to go, and I wanted to find out a bit more before I book her in.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Of course. How old is she?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: She's ten. I saw a poster that said it's for children from 8 up to 14. Is that right?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Ah, that poster's a bit out of date, I'm afraid. We used to take older children, but now it's 8 to 12, so she'd be absolutely fine.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Great. And what sort of things do they do?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Every morning there's tennis, and then a second sport. Last year that was swimming, but the pool's being repaired this summer, so instead they'll be playing hockey. In the afternoons they can choose between football and athletics.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Oh, she'll love the hockey. She's just started playing it at school.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: And on the last afternoon we finish with a picnic, and families are welcome to come along. We used to put on a sports show, but honestly, the children much prefer the picnic.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: That sounds nice. Right, which weeks are you running?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We've got three weeks in August. The first one, starting on the 4th, is already full, I'm afraid. But there are still places in the week beginning Monday the 11th, and in the last week, from the 18th.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Hmm, we're away on holiday from the 16th, so it'd have to be the one starting on the 11th.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Fine. So that runs from Monday the 11th to Friday the 15th.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: And how much is it for the week?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The full price is £150. But if you're a member of the leisure centre, it comes down to £135.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: We are, yes. We've got a family membership.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Then it's £135. There was an early booking rate of £120, but that finished at the end of May, unfortunately.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Never mind. What time does it start each day?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Activities start at nine and finish at half past three. But lots of parents work, so you can drop your child off from 8.15, and there's someone to look after them until things begin.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: That's helpful. I start work at nine myself. And what does she need to bring?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: A packed lunch, because we don't provide food, and trainers, of course. Sun cream's a good idea too. And every child must have a cap, as they're outside most of the day. Some children bring sunglasses, but they often get broken, so we'd rather they didn't.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Right, I'll make sure she's got one. Can I book her in now?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Yes, I'll just fill in the form. What's your daughter's name?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Isla Thackray. That's I-S-L-A, and the surname is T-H-A-C-K-R-A-Y.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thank you. And could I check her date of birth? We need it for the insurance.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: It's the 3rd of March, 2015.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely. And what's your home address?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: It's 27 Melbury Road. That's M-E-L-B-U-R-Y. It's just behind the station.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Got it. Does Isla have any medical conditions or allergies we should know about?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: She had asthma when she was younger, but she's grown out of that now. The only thing is nuts. She's allergic to them, so she has to be careful.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Don't worry, we're a nut-free camp anyway, but I'll make a note of it. And a phone number for emergencies?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Could you put my wife's mobile? I'm a builder, so I don't always hear my phone on site. Hers is 07700 900 518.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's right.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely. Last thing. How did you hear about the camp? We like to know which advertising works.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Well, I saw that old poster at the leisure centre, but it was actually the school newsletter that made me ring. There was a piece about you in it last week.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely, I'll put that down. I'll text your wife the booking confirmation and payment details this afternoon.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Perfect. Thanks very much for your help.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: You're welcome. Bye.
turns.speaker: coordinator

parts.title: Safety talk for new trampers

turns.text: Kia ora everyone, and welcome along. I'm Dougal Fraser, and I've been leading trips for the Canterbury Ridge Tramping Club for about twelve years now. Tonight's all about staying safe out in the hills, so grab a cuppa and get comfy.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: First, a quick word about your first trip with us. Normally we'd take new members up to Arthur's Pass, but there are roadworks on the highway all month, so that's off. We do evening walks on the Port Hills, but those are for people who've already been out with us. So your first one will be over on Banks Peninsula, on Saturday the twenty-third.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, planning. When people plan a tramp, they tend to spend ages on how hard the track's graded, or on sorting out who's driving. Both matter, sure. But the one thing I insist on, above everything else, is that you leave details of your route and the time you expect to be out by. No exceptions.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, who do you leave those details with? Years ago we used to drop a form in at the Department of Conservation visitor centre, but they stopped accepting them a while back. And please don't send it to our club secretary, because she can't be by the phone around the clock. Give it to a friend or someone in your family, someone you trust to raise the alarm if you're not back.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Okay, equipment, starting with your feet. The club has a few rain jackets members can borrow, but we haven't got any boots, sorry. And I'm not going to inspect everyone's footwear at the car park either. What I will ask is that you don't turn up in boots straight out of the box. Wear them around town for a couple of weeks first, so they're properly broken in.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Next, the weather, which in this part of the country can change in minutes. Lots of you will just check the weather app on your phone. The club website does post a forecast link too, but it's often a day out of date. The one we rely on is the mountain forecast on MetService, because it's specific to the high country.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: So what happens if the weather turns on us halfway through a trip? Most people assume we'd just turn round and go back the way we came. Actually, that's often not the safest choice, because you'd be heading back over exposed ridges. Sitting it out and waiting isn't great either, as you get cold really fast. What we normally do is drop down to a lower track, an escape route we'll have worked out in advance.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: And rivers. Crossings are one of the biggest risks for trampers in this country. Our rule used to be that you didn't cross if the water was above waist height, but that's far too deep when it's flowing fast. So now it's simple: if it's higher than your knees, nobody goes in. People ask whether linking arms makes it okay, and it helps, but it doesn't change the rule.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, let's talk about what goes in your pack. The club carries a personal locator beacon and the main first-aid kit, and the trip leader looks after both, so you don't need your own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: But every single person must bring a head torch, even on a day walk, because delays happen. You'll also need a spare warm layer, like a fleece, however sunny it looks when you set off. A paper map's handy, but I'll always have one, so that's up to you.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, emergencies. If someone gets hurt, don't move them unless they're in danger where they are. And don't give them anything to eat or drink yet, until we know how bad it is. What you should do is get something underneath them and keep them warm, because the cold's the real danger out there. Then, if it's serious, we set off the beacon, which sends our exact position to the rescue services.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: In the old days, you'd send one person running out to get help. We don't do that any more. We keep the group together, and nobody heads off on their own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Last thing: next Thursday's session. We'd hoped to have a volunteer from LandSAR, the search and rescue people, but they can't come till next month. So instead we'll head out onto the field behind the hall for some map and compass practice. And I'll give you a proper demonstration of how the beacon works, since any of you might need to set it off one day.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: The first-aid course is separate, by the way. That's a weekend in March, and it costs $85. And no, sorry, there's no gear sale this year. Right, any questions?
turns.speaker: leader

parts.title: A wetland field trip report

turns.text: Come in, Chloe, Lachlan. Have a seat. So you wanted to talk about your report on the Millers Creek wetland trip?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Yes, thanks, Dr Ambrose. We've got a draft of the observations section, but we wanted to check we're on the right track before we go any further.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure. Walk me through what you saw. Start at the beginning.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so we started on the boardwalk near the car park. We'd expected to hear frogs along there, because the guidebook mentions them, but it was totally silent. What we did notice was heaps of chip packets and drink bottles jammed under the planks. People obviously just drop them on the way in.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's pretty common near access points. And then?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then we went to the bird hide. Lachlan was convinced he'd spotted a dead fish floating near it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: It turned out to be a bit of bark.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. But the exciting thing was a pair of swamp harriers, no, sorry, purple swamphens, sitting on a nest in the rushes just in front of the hide. We watched them for about twenty minutes.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great. What about the inlet channel, where the creek comes in?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: We took the temperature there because we assumed it'd be warmer, with the water being so shallow, but the readings were completely normal. The water itself, though, was a sort of brown colour, really thick with sediment. It'd rained heavily the night before, so that probably washed soil in from the farms upstream.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Probably, yes. You'll want to mention the rainfall in the report.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay. Then the reed beds, which were the highlight for me. As soon as we got close, the croaking was unbelievable. We counted well over forty of them in a ten-metre stretch.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Wow. And did you get down to the mudflats?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: We did. We'd been told to look out for an introduced weed there, but we couldn't find any at all. Instead there were several fish lying on the mud, and they weren't moving. Maybe five or six of them.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, that could be low oxygen. Note it, but don't speculate too much.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And the last stop was the eastern pond. Our tutor last year said the bank there was collapsing, but honestly it looked solid to us. What we did find was a big patch of alligator weed, which isn't native. It was brought in from South America.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's a significant finding. The parks people will definitely want to know about that.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, now you said in your email that there were some problems with the data.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Yeah. The water samples from the first day are pretty much useless. We thought at first the bottles had been contaminated, but it turned out nobody had calibrated the pH meter before we used it, so all the readings were off.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That happens more than you'd think. Did you repeat them?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: On day two, yes. But the bird counts on the second morning were a problem too. It wasn't the wind, that had dropped by then, but there was heavy fog until about nine, and we could barely see across the water.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So you probably undercounted. One way to deal with that is to check your numbers against an outside source. The university does have some old records, but they're over a decade old. I'd go to the local council instead. They run annual bird surveys and the data is free to download.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Oh, good, we didn't know that.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So where do we talk about all this in the report? We'd put it in the conclusion.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I wouldn't. The conclusion should be about what you found. Give the data problems their own heading, a limitations section, straight after the results. Be honest about them. Markers respect that.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay. And for the site description, we've written about two pages so far.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's too much. Readers don't need a long paragraph about where every pond is. Cut most of it and include an annotated map, with your sampling points marked on it. Photos are nice, but they can go in the appendix.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Fair enough. And the length is still three thousand words?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Actually, no, the department cut it this year. The maximum is now 2,500 words, not counting the appendix and references.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, that'll make things easier, actually. Thanks so much, Dr Ambrose.
turns.speaker: student_a

parts.title: Urban heat islands

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're moving on from transportation to something that affects almost every city on this continent, and that's what's known as the urban heat island. Put simply, it's the way built-up areas end up noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: On a summer day, a downtown core can be several degrees hotter than nearby farmland. Now, most people assume the difference is biggest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun's at its strongest. In fact, that's not really the case. The gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it stored up during the day, while rural areas cool down fast.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So why does this happen? Well, the first reason is the materials we build with. Brick and concrete both soak up heat, but the real culprit is asphalt, the dark material on our roads and parking lots. On a sunny afternoon, it can get hot enough to burn your hand.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second reason is the lack of vegetation. Plants draw water up from the soil and release it through their leaves, and as that water turns to vapor, it takes heat out of the air. This process, evaporation, is basically nature's air conditioning. Replace a meadow with a shopping mall, and you lose it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Third, there's the shape of the city itself. When tall buildings line narrow streets, you get what planners call canyons. Sunlight bounces from wall to wall instead of escaping, and the wind can't get through to carry the warm air away.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And finally, there's waste heat from cars, from factories, and, rather ironically, from air conditioners pumping hot air out onto the street. So that's four causes, all working together.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so what are the effects? Let's start with health. Heat waves are one of the deadliest kinds of extreme weather in North America, and the people most at risk aren't always the ones you'd expect.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Young children are vulnerable, yes, but the biggest danger is to older people who live alone, often in top-floor apartments, with nobody checking on them. Many of them don't realize how dangerous the heat is until it's too late.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Heat also makes air quality worse. Higher temperatures speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, which irritates the lungs and is especially bad for people with asthma. So on the hottest days, the air is also at its most harmful to breathe.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then there's energy. When it's hot, everybody turns up the air conditioning at the same time, usually between about four and, well, seven in the evening. Electricity bills go up, of course, but the bigger worry is the power grid. If demand gets too high, the utilities simply can't keep up, and that's when you see blackouts, which switch off the very air conditioning that vulnerable people depend on.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So what can cities do about all this? The most obvious answer is trees. A mature tree shades the ground and cools the air through its leaves, as we discussed.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But where you plant it really matters. A lot of homeowners think the south side of a building is best. Actually, research shows the biggest savings come from trees on the west side, because they block the low, intense sun of late afternoon. That's exactly when buildings are at their hottest.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The challenge is that city streets aren't a great place for a tree to grow. Under the sidewalk, the soil is packed hard and full of pipes and cables, so there's very little room for roots to spread. That's why so many street trees die young, and why some cities now build special underground frames that hold loose soil beneath the pavement.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second solution is what we call cool roofs. A normal dark roof can reach over 150 degrees Fahrenheit in summer. A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, that sends most of the sunlight straight back into the sky. New York, for example, has had volunteers treating thousands of rooftops this way.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Cool roofs can go on almost any building, but they're cheapest and simplest on flat roofs, the kind you see on warehouses, schools and apartment blocks. On a steep roof, the work's harder and more dangerous. And frankly, a lot of homeowners just don't like the look of a bright white roof on their house.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There is one drawback, though. In places with cold winters, like Chicago or Toronto, a cool roof reflects away sunlight you'd actually like to have in January. So your heating costs can go up slightly in the colder months. In most cases, though, the summer savings are far bigger than that winter penalty.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, I'll stop there for today. For next week, I'd like you to look at a map of your own neighborhood and think about where the hottest spots might be, and which of these solutions would suit them. We'll compare notes in the seminar.
turns.speaker: lecturer

groups.title: Urban Heat Islands

questions.prompt: Temperature difference between city and countryside is greatest at ______
questions.evidence: The gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night

explanation.en: The lecturer says many people think the difference is biggest in the afternoon, but it is actually widest at night, when the city releases stored heat.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что многие считают, будто разница больше всего днём ("afternoon"), но на самом деле она максимальна ночью ("night"), когда город отдаёт накопленное тепло.
explanation.uk: Лекторка каже, що багато хто вважає, ніби різниця найбільша вдень ("afternoon"), але насправді вона найбільша вночі ("night"), коли місто віддає накопичене тепло.

questions.prompt: Dark surfaces, especially ______, absorb and store heat
questions.evidence: the real culprit is asphalt, the dark material on our roads and parking lots

explanation.en: Brick and concrete are mentioned too, but the lecturer calls asphalt, the dark material on roads, the real culprit.
explanation.ru: Кирпич и бетон ("brick", "concrete") тоже упоминаются, но настоящим виновником лектор называет асфальт ("asphalt"), тёмное покрытие дорог.
explanation.uk: Цеглу й бетон ("brick", "concrete") теж згадано, але справжнім винуватцем лекторка називає асфальт ("asphalt"), темне покриття доріг.

questions.prompt: Fewer plants means less cooling through ______
questions.evidence: This process, evaporation, is basically nature's air conditioning.

explanation.en: Plants release water through their leaves, and evaporation of this water cools the air. Cities with few plants lose this cooling.
explanation.ru: Растения выделяют воду через листья, и её испарение ("evaporation") охлаждает воздух. В городах, где мало растений, такого охлаждения нет.
explanation.uk: Рослини виділяють воду через листя, і її випаровування ("evaporation") охолоджує повітря. У містах, де мало рослин, такого охолодження немає.

questions.prompt: Tall buildings and narrow streets form ______ that trap heat
questions.evidence: you get what planners call canyons

explanation.en: Tall buildings along narrow streets create 'canyons', where sunlight bounces between walls and wind cannot remove the warm air.
explanation.ru: Высокие здания вдоль узких улиц образуют «каньоны» ("canyons"): солнечный свет отражается от стены к стене, а ветер не может унести тёплый воздух.
explanation.uk: Високі будівлі вздовж вузьких вулиць утворюють «каньйони» ("canyons"): сонячне світло відбивається від стіни до стіни, а вітер не може винести тепле повітря.

questions.prompt: Greatest health risk: elderly people who live ______
questions.evidence: the biggest danger is to older people who live alone

explanation.en: Young children are mentioned as vulnerable, but the biggest danger is to older people living alone with nobody checking on them.
explanation.ru: Маленькие дети ("young children") тоже упоминаются как уязвимая группа, но больше всего опасность грозит пожилым людям ("older people"), которые живут одни и которых никто не проведывает.
explanation.uk: Малих дітей ("young children") теж згадано як вразливу групу, але найбільша небезпека загрожує літнім людям ("older people"), які живуть самі й яких ніхто не навідує.

questions.prompt: Heat increases levels of ground-level ______, which harms the lungs
questions.evidence: the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone

explanation.en: Higher temperatures speed up the reactions that create ground-level ozone, which irritates the lungs.
explanation.ru: Высокая температура ускоряет реакции, в результате которых образуется приземный озон ("ozone"), раздражающий лёгкие.
explanation.uk: Висока температура прискорює реакції, унаслідок яких утворюється приземний озон ("ozone"), що подразнює легені.

questions.prompt: Very high demand for electricity may cause ______
questions.evidence: that's when you see blackouts

explanation.en: Higher electricity bills are mentioned, but the bigger worry is that the grid cannot keep up, which leads to blackouts.
explanation.ru: Рост счетов за электричество тоже упоминается, но главная проблема в том, что энергосеть не справляется с нагрузкой, а это приводит к отключениям ("blackouts").
explanation.uk: Зростання рахунків за електрику теж згадано, але головна проблема в тому, що енергомережа не витримує навантаження, а це призводить до відключень ("blackouts").

questions.prompt: Trees give the greatest benefit on the ______ side of a building
questions.evidence: the biggest savings come from trees on the west side

explanation.en: Many homeowners think the south side is best, but research shows trees on the west side save the most because they block the late-afternoon sun.
explanation.ru: Многие владельцы домов считают, что лучше всего южная сторона ("south"), но исследования показывают, что больше всего экономят деревья с западной стороны ("west"), потому что они закрывают дом от солнца в конце дня.
explanation.uk: Багато власників будинків вважають, що найкраще південна сторона ("south"), але дослідження показують, що найбільше заощаджують дерева із західного боку ("west"), бо вони затуляють будинок від сонця наприкінці дня.

questions.prompt: Street trees often have too little space for their ______
questions.evidence: there's very little room for roots to spread

explanation.en: Under sidewalks the soil is hard and full of pipes and cables, so roots have little room to spread.
explanation.ru: Под тротуарами ("sidewalks") почва твёрдая, в ней полно труб и кабелей, поэтому корням почти негде разрастаться.
explanation.uk: Під тротуарами ("sidewalks") ґрунт твердий, у ньому повно труб і кабелів, тому корінню майже ніде розростатися.

questions.prompt: Cool roofs: a reflective ______ is applied to the roof
questions.evidence: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating

explanation.en: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, which sends sunlight back into the sky.
explanation.ru: На «холодную крышу» ("cool roof") наносят отражающее покрытие ("reflective coating"), обычно белое, которое отправляет солнечный свет обратно в небо.
explanation.uk: На «холодний дах» ("cool roof") наносять відбивне покриття ("reflective coating"), зазвичай біле, яке відправляє сонячне світло назад у небо.

parts.title: Renting a flat in Brunswick

turns.text: Good morning, Northside Property, Kylie Brannigan speaking. How can I help you?

turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: And could you spell the surname for me?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Sure. It's Templeton. T-E-M-P-L-E-T-O-N.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thanks, Josh. And do you have the full address of the flat you're interested in?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Yeah, it's 22 Wattle Road. That's W-A-T-T-L-E.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.speaker: agent

turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: It's on the second floor... sorry, no, I'm thinking of the one next door. This one's on the third floor, and there's a lift, so you won't be carrying your shopping up the stairs.

turns.text: Ah, that was the old price, I'm afraid. The owner's put it up since then, so it's now $485 a week. That's still pretty reasonable for the area, though.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Okay. And does that cover any of the bills?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Ah, I don't finish work until five on Thursdays. Is anything later possible?

turns.text: Hmm, how about 5.30? That's the latest I can do, I'm afraid.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: 5.30 is perfect. Thursday at 5.30, then.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Of course. Transport's very good. The nearest tram stop is only about two minutes' walk from the building, and the tram gets you into the city in about 25 minutes. There's a train station too, and the train's quicker, around 15 minutes, but the station's a fair walk away.

turns.text: I'll probably take the tram, then. What about shopping?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There's a big supermarket on Sydney Road. It's right next to the bank, and opposite the library. And it's open until 10 pm every night, which is handy if you work late.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Great. I like to keep fit, actually. Is there anywhere outdoors to exercise?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Well, there's a park about five minutes' walk away. It's got tennis courts, and an outdoor swimming pool as well. There used to be a running track, but they've turned that into a playground.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Sounds good. And is there a gym nearby?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There's one right above the supermarket. A membership is $45 a month. Or if you'd rather not sign up, you can pay $12 each time you go.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: $45 a month isn't bad at all. Anything else worth knowing about?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There's a farmers' market in the grounds of the primary school. It used to run on Saturdays, but it's moved to Sunday mornings now. Lots of fresh fruit and veg, and great coffee.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: That's fine. Thanks so much, Kylie. See you on Thursday.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: See you then, Josh. Just give me a ring on this number if anything changes.

parts.title: A reopened science museum

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashbury Science Museum. My name's Owen Ratcliffe, and I'm one of the guides here. As you probably know, we've been closed for nearly two years, well, twenty-two months to be exact, while the building was renovated, so it's lovely to see visitors again. I'll start with the ground floor, and then I'll tell you about the new galleries upstairs.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, you've all got a copy of the ground-floor plan, I hope. We're standing just inside the main entrance, facing north. On your left is the ticket desk, and on your right is the shop.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, most of you will want somewhere to leave coats and bags. The room beside the ticket desk, to the west, looks as if it might be the cloakroom, but it's actually staff offices. The cloakroom's on the other side, right next to the shop, just beyond it to the east.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Then, if you walk straight up the main corridor, you'll come to a crossroads where it meets the long corridor running east to west. Just before that crossroads, there are two large rooms facing each other. The one on your left is the Energy Zone, which, I'm sorry to say, won't open until the summer. The one on your right is the Flight Gallery, with the old biplane hanging from the ceiling, and that's open now.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: OK. At the crossroads, turn left and walk west, right to the end of the corridor. The room on your left, at the very end, is where we'll hold our temporary exhibitions. The first one's about volcanoes, and it's well worth a look. It runs until the end of September, and there's no extra charge for it.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Directly opposite it, on the right-hand side, is the picnic room. If you've brought your own sandwiches, that's the place to eat them. Please don't eat them in the café, which is just north of the picnic room. The café staff get rather upset about that!
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, for families with small children. The play area used to be in the basement, but we've moved it up here. It's the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts. The lifts are at the far end of the main corridor, by the way, so if you're pushing a buggy, that's the easiest way to reach it.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: And finally, the toilets. Go back to the crossroads, and this time follow the long corridor east instead of west. Right at the end, the door on your right is the toilets. Opposite them, on your left, is the lecture theatre, where there are free talks every afternoon.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, that's the ground floor. Now for the exciting part: the six brand-new galleries on the first floor. Every one of them has something hands-on, so let me quickly tell you what you can actually do in each.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Let's start with the Space Gallery. People always ask me if there's a telescope they can look through. I'm afraid there isn't; there simply wasn't room. But you can climb into a full-size copy of a space capsule, and with the screens and controls inside, it feels as if you're really docking with the space station.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Next door is the Medicine Gallery. Most of it's glass cases, as you'd expect, but there's a table in the middle where you can put on gloves and pick up genuine surgical tools from the 1800s. They're surprisingly heavy.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Then there's the Engineering Hall. You'll see a big robot arm in there, and children always want a go with it, but it's behind glass, so nobody can operate it, I'm afraid. What you can do is put together a little bridge out of card and straws, and then add weights to find out how much it'll hold before it falls down.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: The Sound Studio is great fun, and it's especially popular with teenagers. There's a booth where you talk into a microphone, and it keeps a copy of what you've said so you can listen to yourself afterwards. Most people are shocked by what they sound like!
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: On the Chemistry Stage, you can't touch anything, for obvious safety reasons. But at 11 am, 1 pm and 3 pm each day, one of our scientists mixes chemicals in front of the audience, and you can watch the colours change and the smoke appear.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: And last of all, the Climate Gallery. Along one wall there are touch screens with ten questions about the weather and the planet, and at the end, it tells you how many you got right. See if you can beat your children's score! Right, any questions before we head upstairs?
turns.speaker: guide

explanation.en: The cloakroom is just east of the shop. The room beside the ticket desk looks like it, but the guide says it is staff offices.

explanation.uk: "Picnic room" розташована навпроти зали "temporary exhibitions", праворуч, якщо йти на захід, і одразу на південь від кафе.

questions.evidence: It's the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts.

explanation.en: The play area is the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts. It used to be in the basement, but it is now on the ground floor.

parts.title: Choosing a research method

turns.text: Hi Jordan. Okay, so Professor Reyes wants our method proposal by Friday, and we still haven't picked between interviews and a questionnaire. We really need to decide today.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I know. I've been going back and forth on it. What's your feeling?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Honestly, I keep coming back to interviews. Everyone says they give you richer, more detailed data, and that's true. But for me the big thing is that you can follow up. If someone says they just deal with stress, you can ask them to explain what they actually mean.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. And people probably feel more relaxed chatting than filling in a form, too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, I'm not so sure about that, actually. A lot of students would find it pretty awkward talking to a stranger about stress. Anyway, what about you? You were leaning toward a questionnaire, weren't you?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was. I mean, obviously you can reach way more people, and the results are a lot easier to analyze. But what really convinces me is that nobody has to give their name. With a topic like exam stress, people might not admit how badly they're coping if they're sitting across from you.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's a fair point. And there's the time issue. Remember what Professor Reyes said in class on Tuesday? I was half expecting her to tell us our topic was too broad, but she didn't. What she did say was that transcribing and coding interviews always takes about three times longer than students plan for.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I remember that. Though I read somewhere that online surveys get really low response rates, so questionnaires aren't exactly a quick fix either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. So what if we did both? A questionnaire first, and then interviews with five or six people afterward?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: In an ideal world, sure. But with only eight weeks, sorry, seven weeks now, I don't think we can manage it. How about this: we go with the questionnaire, but we add two or three open questions at the end, where people can answer in their own words. That way we still get some of that detail you wanted.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, I can live with that. It's a good compromise. Now, who are we asking? Should we open it up to everyone, all years?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's way too wide for a project this size. I did think about psychology students, since they'd be easy to find, but they'd probably guess what we're looking for, and that could skew the answers.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good point. So let's just do first-years, and only the ones living in residence. They're all dealing with their first set of finals, and they're easy to reach.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Perfect. Okay, so let's map out the steps so we can put them in the proposal.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. Step one is writing the questions. I really don't want to make everything up from scratch, so I think we should adapt items from published studies. That coping scale from week three would be a good start.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. Then we need to check the wording works. I was going to try it out on my roommates, but they'd just tell us it's great. Let's test it on some classmates from the methods course instead. They'll actually be critical.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good idea. After that, we fix anything confusing, and then it has to be approved. I assumed Professor Reyes could just sign it off, but no, anything involving human participants has to go to the ethics board.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Okay. And that can take a couple of weeks, so we should submit it early. Once it's approved, we recruit people. I asked about using the residence email list, but apparently that's only for official notices. So we'll put up flyers in each of the residence halls.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sounds good. And for handing out the paper copies, I'd thought about the library, but they don't allow anything like that inside. So we'll set up a table in the dining hall at lunchtime. It's the busiest spot on campus, so we should get plenty of people.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great. Then, once we've collected them all, we enter the responses into a spreadsheet. We can move everything into the statistics software later, but getting it all typed up comes first.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: And then the last step is presenting it. I'd assumed we'd do a slideshow, but Professor Reyes wants every group to make a poster and explain it to the class in the final week.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Got it. Okay, I'll start writing this up tonight and send it to you tomorrow.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Perfect. Thanks, Jordan.
turns.speaker: student_a

parts.title: How migrating birds navigate

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're carrying on with animal behaviour, and I want to look at one of the big puzzles in zoology: how migrating birds find their way. Think of the bar-tailed godwit. Every September it leaves Alaska and flies non-stop to places like the Firth of Thames, here in New Zealand, a journey of over eleven thousand kilometres. So how on earth does it know where it's going?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's start with the sun. In the 1950s a German scientist, Gustav Kramer, noticed something odd about caged starlings. When the season for migrating came round, they didn't sit still. They fluttered and hopped about, and they kept facing the direction they'd normally fly in. This is what we now call migratory restlessness, and it gave researchers a really handy way to measure which way a bird wants to go.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Kramer then asked whether the birds were actually using the sun. He thought about moving the cage, or putting lamps around it, but in the end he went for something simpler. He used mirrors to make the sun appear to be in a different position. And sure enough, the starlings turned to face a new direction, by just about the same amount he'd shifted the sun.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, there's a complication here. The sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird can't just fly towards it. It has to adjust for the time, and to do that it needs an internal clock. Researchers showed this by keeping birds under artificial lights that were switched on six hours late. Their clocks were thrown out, and they headed off in the wrong direction, just as you'd predict.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But lots of birds migrate at night. So what about the stars? In the 1960s an American researcher, Stephen Emlen, studied a small songbird called the indigo bunting. People often assume he took them to an observatory, but no, he tested them inside a planetarium, where he could control exactly which stars they saw.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What he found was fascinating. Young buntings don't come with a star map built in. Instead, as they grow, they learn which part of the sky the stars turn around, the centre of rotation, which in the northern hemisphere is close to the Pole Star. And when Emlen made the planetarium sky rotate around a different star, the birds treated that star as north.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, the third cue is the earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s Wolfgang Wiltschko put European robins in cages surrounded by electric coils, which let him change the magnetic field. The robins changed direction too. But here's the surprising part. Robins don't sense whether the field points north or south, the way a compass needle does. What they detect is the angle of the field lines in relation to the ground.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So where's the sensor? For a long time people thought it was tiny bits of iron in the beak. That idea hasn't really held up, I'm afraid. The current theory is that it involves light-sensitive proteins in the eye, which may mean that birds can actually see the magnetic field in some way.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There's a nice example of how sensitive this system is. A team in Oldenburg, in Germany, found their robins couldn't orient at all in wooden huts on the university campus. The cause turned out to be weak electrical noise from equipment around the city. Once the huts were lined with aluminium and grounded, the birds oriented perfectly again.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK. Those three compasses get a bird into the right general area. But near the end of a journey, many birds switch to what they can see. They pick up familiar landmarks, things like coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges, much as you would on a road trip down the South Island.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Homing pigeons give us good evidence for this. Researchers at Oxford fitted pigeons with GPS trackers and found they flew along the same routes again and again. I'd expected them to follow railway lines, which are straight and easy to see, but in fact the birds mostly followed major roads, even turning at junctions.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, smell, which was the most controversial idea. In Italy in the 1970s, Floriano Papi worked with pigeons that had lost their sense of smell. Near their loft they were fine. But when they were released at unfamiliar sites, a long way off, most of them never made it home.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Plenty of scientists doubted this, partly because birds were thought to have a weak sense of smell. Then, in 2015, a study looked at Scopoli's shearwaters, which are seabirds. Some had their sense of smell blocked for a short time. Over open ocean they got lost, but they could still navigate when they were flying along the coast, where they could use what they saw.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So what's the overall picture? Birds don't rely on a single system. They combine several, and switch between them depending on the weather and where they are. That's why they're so reliable.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: For next week, I'd like you to read about a newer problem. We used to worry mainly about noise from cities, but the bigger threat to night-flying birds seems to be light pollution, which can draw them off course. We'll look at what can be done about it. Thanks, everyone.
turns.speaker: lecturer

parts.title: Welcome to the university library

turns.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Hartwell Library. My name's Dana Whitmore, and I'm one of the librarians here. Over the next twenty minutes or so, I'll tell you how borrowing works, where you can study, and what kind of help you can get. So, let's start with borrowing.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Your student card is also your library card, so there's nothing extra to sign up for. Now, a lot of you will have heard that undergraduates can take out ten items at a time. That was true until last year, but the limit's now fifteen. Graduate students can have twenty, but for you, it's fifteen.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, what if you keep something too long? We actually got rid of daily fines a couple of years ago, so you won't be paying a few cents a day. What happens instead is that your account gets frozen, so you can't check out anything else until the late item comes back. We'll only send you a bill for the replacement cost if something's more than six weeks overdue.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Right, course reserves. These are books your professors have put aside because the whole class needs them, and they're kept behind the main service desk. Some of you might think you can only read them inside the building. That used to be the rule, but these days you can take them out for up to four hours at a time. And you don't need to request them online or anything; just ask at the desk.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Let's move on to online resources. We subscribe to thousands of journals and e-books, and you can get to all of them from home. A few years ago, you had to install special software on your laptop to do that. Now you just sign in through the library website with the same email and password you use for everything else on campus. There's no need to register with us separately.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And if we don't have something, we can borrow it from another library for you. That's called an interlibrary loan, and it's free. Journal articles are quickest; they usually arrive by email in two or three days. Books take a bit longer, normally about a week, although something rare or very old can take up to a month.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: We also run workshops all semester, on things like citing sources and searching databases. Some new students also rush to book one-on-one appointments with a librarian in their first week. But honestly, the first thing I'd ask you to do is the online orientation tutorial on our website. It only takes about twenty minutes, and it'll answer most of your questions before you even have them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, now let me tell you about some of the spaces and services you'll see as we walk around. First, the group study rooms on the third floor. You can reserve them on our website up to seven days in advance, and I'd recommend that, because they fill up fast. And there's a myth that they're only for final-year students. That's not true at all; anyone can book them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Next, the silent reading room on the fourth floor. It's completely quiet, and to keep it that way, you're not allowed to bring bags inside. There are lockers just outside the door for that. Some people ask if it stays open all night during exams. It doesn't, I'm afraid; that's the twenty-four-hour lounge on the ground floor.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: If your own laptop breaks down, don't panic. You can borrow one of ours from the service desk, using your student card. They're very popular, so the rule is they have to come back to the desk before we close that same evening. You can't keep them overnight.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Then there's the writing center, where tutors help you plan and improve your essays. If you've seen old maps of the building, they show it on the second floor. But over the summer it moved down to the basement, next to the computer lab, so that's where you'll find it now.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Printing. Printers are on every floor, and you pay with your student card. Each semester, the first hundred pages are free, so you don't pay anything until you've used those up. After that it's ten cents a page, sorry, eight cents, for black and white.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And finally, the subject librarians. Every department has one, and they're the people to talk to about research for your assignments. During the day you can drop by their offices on the first floor, but a lot of students have classes then, so they also offer video calls in the evenings, until about nine. You'll find the links on the library website.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, that's the overview. Let's head upstairs, and I'll show you the third floor first.
turns.speaker: librarian

parts.title: A bakery case study

turns.text: Right, Callum, shall we make a start on the bakery case study? The report's due on Friday.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, good idea. I've read it twice now. Shall we begin with what Hartley's Bakery got right?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: OK. At first I thought the loyalty card was one of their strengths, but then I noticed they gave it up after about three months, because hardly anyone used it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right, so that doesn't really count. What about the location? It's near the station, isn't it?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Well, it's on a side street behind the station, so most commuters walk straight past it. If anything, I'd put that under problems.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. And staff training? I thought they had a proper programme.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: The owner talks about wanting one, but it never actually happened. They just learn on the job.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: OK. For me, the real strength is where everything comes from. All their flour is milled about five miles away and the eggs come from a farm nearby. And then there's Instagram: the owner posts photos of the morning bake every day, and that's what brings in most new customers.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Agreed, those are the two to focus on. So, problems. The case study mentions that big supermarket that opened on the ring road last year.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yes, but the owner says her sales hardly changed after it opened, so I don't think that's a real issue. And the online reviews are nearly all five stars, so it's not about quality either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. What struck me was the bills. Running the ovens from four in the morning means their electricity costs have almost doubled in two years. And then there's how much they throw away. Around a fifth of everything they bake is still on the shelves at closing time.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's a lot. I'd expected them to say they couldn't find trained bakers, but apparently recruitment has been easy.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. So what are we going to recommend? I wondered about moving to the high street, where more people pass by.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The rent there's three times as much, though. They'd never afford it. What about staying open into the evening?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That means paying staff for extra hours, and the area's pretty quiet after six. I don't think so.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So I'd go for two things. First, replacing the old ovens with energy-efficient ones. There's a government grant that would cover half the cost. Second, selling whatever's left at the end of the day at half price, maybe through one of those food-waste apps.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yes, that tackles both of the big problems directly. Should we suggest a marketing consultant as well?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I don't think they need one. Their Instagram's already doing that job for free.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. OK, the second section is what to do with each product. Let's start with the sourdough.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: It's their bestseller. It sells out by eleven most mornings, and at £3.20 a loaf it's cheaper than anywhere else in town.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I was going to say they should just bake more of it, but that means more energy. I reckon they could easily charge more, and people would still buy it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. Next, the cinnamon buns. They fly off the shelves on Saturdays and Sundays, but from Monday to Friday nearly half of them end up in the bin.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: So should they stop making them altogether?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, they're far too popular for that. They should just bake them for the weekend and leave them out the rest of the time.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Makes sense. Then there are the celebration cakes. At the moment you have to go into the shop to order one, and the owner admits she loses customers because of that.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd thought about suggesting an advert in the local paper, but that's a bit old-fashioned. People want to choose a design and pay from home, so they should set up a way to order them through the website.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good. Sandwiches next. They're really the part of the business that loses money. The fillings have to be bought fresh every day, there's the café next door competing, and they make about 10p on each one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was going to say cut the price, but you're right, there's no point. Let's just say they should stop making them completely.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: What about the gluten-free brownies? Hardly anyone buys them in the shop.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, but the case study says two cafés in town have asked about stocking them. So instead of relying on the shop, they could sell them to cafés and offices in the area.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's better than my idea, which was just to change the packaging. And the meat pies?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: They're a bit tricky. They make thirty a day, but only about twenty get sold. They're worth keeping, but they should make fewer of them.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: And finally, the hot drinks. A coffee's only £1.50, which is about a pound less than the chains charge.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd say leave those as they are. Actually, no. The beans come from a local roaster, so customers would happily pay a bit more. Let's put that down too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. I'll write up the products section tonight and send it over tomorrow, Callum.
turns.speaker: student_a
