segments.text: Part 4. You will hear a social history lecturer giving a talk about the development of the bicycle and its effects on society. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

parts.title: The bicycle and social change

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something most of you probably rode as kids without a second thought: the bicycle. I'll start by tracing how its design developed during the nineteenth century. Then, since this is a social history course, we'll look at what it did to people's working lives, to women's freedom, and to the shape of our cities.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, let's start in Germany in 1817. A man called Karl Drais built what's usually considered the first two-wheeled machine. It had no pedals at all. You sat on it and pushed yourself along with your feet. Now, why did he bother? One popular theory is that after a run of bad harvests, oats became terribly expensive, and lots of horses died or were sold off. So Drais was looking for a way to get around without relying on one.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The next big step came in France in the 1860s, when pedals were fixed directly to the front wheel. These machines were officially called velocipedes, but people gave them a much less flattering name. They had wooden wheels with iron rims, and the streets were often cobbled, so in English they became known as boneshakers. I think you can imagine why.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then, in the 1870s, came the penny-farthing, with that enormous front wheel and tiny back one. People often assume the big wheel was there for comfort, but that wasn't really the point. Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, a bigger wheel meant you travelled further with each turn of the pedals. In other words, more speed. The downside was that a fall from that height could be serious, so the riders were mostly young, athletic men.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The real turning point was the so-called safety bicycle, which appeared in England in 1885. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the rider sat much lower. But the crucial change wasn't the frame. It was that the pedals now drove the back wheel by means of a chain, so you could get good speed without a giant wheel.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: A few years later, in 1887, sorry, 1888, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, John Dunlop, developed the air-filled tyre. He didn't originally have bicycles in mind, actually. He was trying to give his young son a smoother ride on his tricycle. Within a decade, though, these pneumatic tyres were standard on bicycles everywhere.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So by the 1890s you had a machine that was safe, comfortable and, as factories began mass-producing them, increasingly affordable. That's when the great bicycle boom happened, and Australia was very much part of it. Let's turn to work. In the outback, shearers began riding bicycles between sheep stations, sometimes covering hundreds of kilometres. Before that, they'd have walked, or gone on horseback if they could afford a horse.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And on the Western Australian goldfields, around Coolgardie, cyclists were paid to carry letters between the mining camps and the nearest telegraph office. People sometimes assume they carried gold, but that would've been far too risky on a bike in the middle of the desert. Letters, on the other hand, were light, and they were urgent.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, the bicycle probably had its most dramatic effect on women's lives. To ride comfortably, many women gave up the long, heavy skirts of the time. Some wore what were called bloomers, that's B-L-O-O-M-E-R-S, which were loose trousers gathered at the knee. It was a very visible challenge to ideas about how a respectable woman should dress.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But it wasn't only about clothing. A young, unmarried woman was generally expected to have a chaperone with her whenever she went out, usually an older woman from the family who'd keep an eye on her. On a bicycle, she could simply ride off on her own, and a chaperone on foot couldn't possibly keep up. So women gained a kind of independence they'd never had before.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Not everyone approved, of course. Some church leaders complained that cycling kept people away from Sunday services, but that applied to men as much as women. The fiercest criticism of women riding came from doctors, who warned it could damage their health. Some even described a condition called bicycle face, a strained, exhausted expression. Sounds ridiculous now, but it appeared in serious medical journals.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, cities. We tend to think it was the motor car that transformed our roads, but cyclists actually got there first. In the 1890s, cycling clubs in Melbourne and Sydney, and in Britain and America too, lobbied governments to build smoother, better-maintained roads. The clubs also published maps for their members, but those they produced themselves. So cars later benefited from improvements that cyclists had campaigned for.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The other big change was where people lived. Before the bicycle, most working people had to live within walking distance of their jobs, so they crowded into the inner city. With a cheap bike, a clerk or a factory worker could live several kilometres away, out in the suburbs, where housing was cheaper and less crowded. So the bicycle helped start the outward spread of our cities, alongside the early trams, and well before the car.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, that's the overview. Next week, we'll look at how the car pushed the bicycle aside for much of the twentieth century, and why it's now making a comeback.
turns.speaker: lecturer

groups.title: The History of the Bicycle and Social Change

questions.prompt: 1817, Drais's machine: may have been a response to a lack of ______ for transport
questions.evidence: lots of horses died or were sold off

explanation.en: The lecturer says many horses died or were sold, so Drais wanted a way to travel without one. Oats were expensive, but oats are not a means of transport.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что многие лошади ("horses") погибли или были проданы, поэтому Drais хотел найти способ передвигаться без них. Овёс ("oats") действительно был дорогим, но овёс — не средство передвижения.
explanation.uk: Лектор каже, що багато коней ("horses") загинули або були продані, тому Drais хотів знайти спосіб пересуватися без них. Овес ("oats") справді був дорогим, але овес — не засіб пересування.

questions.prompt: 1860s French velocipede: nicknamed ______ in English
questions.evidence: so in English they became known as boneshakers

explanation.en: The official name was velocipede, but in English people called them boneshakers because of the hard wheels on cobbled streets.
explanation.ru: Официальное название было "velocipede", но по-английски их называли "boneshakers" («костотрясы») из-за жёстких колёс на булыжных мостовых.
explanation.uk: Офіційна назва була "velocipede", але англійською їх називали "boneshakers" («кістколами») через тверді колеса на бруківці.

questions.prompt: 1870s penny-farthing: large front wheel gave the rider more ______
questions.evidence: In other words, more speed.

explanation.en: The big wheel meant the bike went further with each turn of the pedals, giving more speed. The lecturer says it was not really about comfort.
explanation.ru: Благодаря большому колесу велосипед проезжал больше за каждый оборот педалей, а значит, ехал быстрее ("speed"). Лектор говорит, что дело было вовсе не в комфорте ("comfort").
explanation.uk: Завдяки великому колесу велосипед проїжджав більше за кожен оберт педалей, а отже, їхав швидше ("speed"). Лектор каже, що річ була зовсім не в комфорті ("comfort").

questions.prompt: 1885 safety bicycle: pedals linked to the back wheel by a ______
questions.evidence: the pedals now drove the back wheel by means of a chain

explanation.en: The key change was that a chain connected the pedals to the back wheel. The lecturer says the important change was not the frame.
explanation.ru: Главное изменение — цепь ("chain") соединила педали с задним колесом. Лектор говорит, что важным изменением была не рама ("frame").
explanation.uk: Головна зміна — ланцюг ("chain") з'єднав педалі із заднім колесом. Лектор каже, що важливою зміною була не рама ("frame").

questions.prompt: 1888, Dunlop's air-filled tyre: first made for his son's ______
questions.evidence: give his young son a smoother ride on his tricycle

explanation.en: Dunlop wanted his son to have a smoother ride on his tricycle. He did not first have bicycles in mind.
explanation.ru: Dunlop хотел, чтобы его сыну было мягче ездить на трёхколёсном велосипеде ("tricycle"). О двухколёсных велосипедах ("bicycles") он поначалу не думал.
explanation.uk: Dunlop хотів, щоб його синові було м'якше їздити на триколісному велосипеді ("tricycle"). Про двоколісні велосипеди ("bicycles") він спочатку не думав.

questions.prompt: Outback shearers cycled long distances between ______
questions.evidence: shearers began riding bicycles between sheep stations

explanation.en: Shearers rode bicycles from one sheep station to another. Before this they walked or used horses.
explanation.ru: Стригали овец ("shearers") ездили на велосипедах от одной овцеводческой фермы ("sheep station") к другой. До этого они ходили пешком или ездили верхом.
explanation.uk: Стригалі овець ("shearers") їздили на велосипедах від однієї вівчарської ферми ("sheep station") до іншої. До цього вони ходили пішки або їздили верхи.

questions.prompt: Cyclists on the goldfields were employed to transport ______
questions.evidence: cyclists were paid to carry letters between the mining camps

explanation.en: The cyclists carried letters, which were light and urgent. The lecturer says they did not carry gold because it was too risky.
explanation.ru: Велосипедисты возили письма ("letters") — они лёгкие и срочные. Лектор говорит, что золото ("gold") они не возили, потому что это было слишком рискованно.
explanation.uk: Велосипедисти возили листи ("letters") — вони легкі й термінові. Лектор каже, що золото ("gold") вони не возили, бо це було надто ризиковано.

questions.prompt: Some female cyclists wore ______ instead of long skirts
questions.evidence: Some wore what were called bloomers, that's B-L-O-O-M-E-R-S

explanation.en: The lecturer spells out the word bloomers, which were loose trousers gathered at the knee.
explanation.ru: Лектор произносит по буквам слово "bloomers" — так назывались свободные брюки, собранные у колена.
explanation.uk: Лектор вимовляє по літерах слово "bloomers" — так називали вільні штани, зібрані біля коліна.

questions.prompt: Young women could now go out without a ______
questions.evidence: she could simply ride off on her own, and a chaperone on foot couldn't possibly keep up

explanation.en: Young women were expected to have a chaperone, but on a bicycle they could ride away alone because the chaperone could not follow on foot.
explanation.ru: Считалось, что молодых женщин должна сопровождать компаньонка ("chaperone"), но на велосипеде они могли уехать одни: пешком компаньонка за ними не поспевала.
explanation.uk: Вважалося, що молодих жінок має супроводжувати компаньйонка ("chaperone"), але на велосипеді вони могли поїхати самі: пішки компаньйонка за ними не встигала.

questions.prompt: Strongest critics of women cycling: ______, who said it was unhealthy
questions.evidence: The fiercest criticism of women riding came from doctors

explanation.en: Doctors gave the strongest criticism and warned about women's health. Church leaders also complained, but about Sunday services, not about women in particular.
explanation.ru: Резче всех критиковали врачи ("doctors"): они предупреждали о вреде для женского здоровья. Церковные деятели ("church leaders") тоже жаловались, но их беспокоили воскресные службы, а не именно женщины.
explanation.uk: Найрізкіше критикували лікарі ("doctors"): вони попереджали про шкоду для жіночого здоров'я. Церковні діячі ("church leaders") теж скаржилися, але їх турбували недільні служби, а не саме жінки.

parts.title: Renting a community garden plot

turns.text: Good morning, Hillcrest Community Garden, this is Donna speaking. How can I help?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Hi, yes. I'm calling about renting a plot. I heard you've got some space this year?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We do, a few plots have opened up. I'll just take some details first, and then I can explain the options. Can I have your name?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Sure, it's Brian Lundgren. That's L-U-N-D-G-R-E-N.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thanks. Let me just write that down. L-U-N-D-G-R-E-N. Got it. And what's your home address, Brian?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: It's 27 Thornton Avenue. T-H-O-R-N-T-O-N. I only moved there in the spring, actually. Before that I was over on Lake Street.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thornton Avenue, OK, that's only a few blocks from us. And the zip code?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: 55418. Oh, no, sorry, that was my old one. It's 55419 now.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: 55419. Thanks. Now, we like to keep track of how people find out about us. Where did you hear about the garden?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Let me think. I thought it was a flyer at the grocery store, but no, it was a poster at the library. I was returning some books and noticed it on the board.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The library, great, our volunteers put those up in March. And have you done any gardening before?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: A little. I've never had a proper backyard, but at my last apartment I grew some lettuce and herbs on the balcony. Just in pots, though.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's still good experience. I'll put down balcony. And what are you hoping to grow here?
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Well, my first thought was tomatoes, but a friend told me everybody grows those and they take over. So I'd say mainly peppers. I cook a lot of Mexican food.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Peppers, good choice, they do well here. Now, all new members have to come to an orientation session before they start. We walk you around and go through the rules. There's one on Sunday afternoon, but that's already full, I'm afraid. The next one is Saturday morning at nine.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Saturday works for me. Do I need to bring anything?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Just a deposit for your gate key. It used to be $15, but we raised it this year, so it's $20 now. You get it back if you return the key when you leave.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: OK, that's fine. So what sizes of plot do you have?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There are three. The small ones are ten feet by ten, and they're $40 a year. Those are all along the east fence, right next to the parking lot, so they're handy if you're carrying heavy bags of soil.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Right. And the medium ones?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Medium plots are twenty feet by ten. Last year they were $60, but the water bill went up, so they're $65 now. And with those, the one big rule is that you have to weed every week. If a plot gets overgrown, we send a warning.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Fair enough. What about the large plots? I might want space for some squash too.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The large ones are $90 a year, but to be honest, they're very popular. There's a waiting list. It used to be about eighteen months, but at the moment it's more like two years.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Two years! I don't think I want to wait that long. I'll go for a medium one. Is there anywhere to keep tools? I don't really want to carry a shovel down the street every time.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Yes, we rent out tool lockers for $25 for the season. We provide gloves and a couple of shared wheelbarrows, but you have to bring your own padlock for the locker. We don't supply those.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: No problem, I've got one at home somewhere. And are hoses allowed?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Hoses, yes, but no sprinklers, they waste too much water. OK, Brian, I'll email you a confirmation, and I'll see you on Saturday.
turns.speaker: coordinator

turns.text: Great, thanks so much, Donna. Bye.
turns.speaker: caller

explanation.uk: Він живе на «Thornton Avenue» і диктує назву по літерах. «Lake Street» — його стара адреса, тож цей варіант неправильний.

questions.prompt: Zip code: ______

explanation.en: He first says 55418 but corrects himself: that was his old zip code, and the new one is 55419.
explanation.ru: Сначала он называет «55418», но тут же поправляется: это его старый почтовый индекс («zip code»), а новый — «55419».
explanation.uk: Спочатку він називає «55418», але одразу виправляється: це його старий поштовий індекс («zip code»), а новий — «55419».

questions.prompt: Found out about the garden from: a poster at the ______
questions.evidence: it was a poster at the library

explanation.en: He first thinks it was a flyer at the grocery store, but then remembers it was a poster at the library.
explanation.ru: Сначала он думает, что это была листовка («flyer») в продуктовом магазине («grocery store»), но потом вспоминает, что это был плакат («poster») в библиотеке («library»).
explanation.uk: Спочатку він думає, що це була листівка («flyer») у продуктовому магазині («grocery store»), але потім згадує, що це був плакат («poster») у бібліотеці («library»).

questions.prompt: Previous experience: grew plants in pots on a ______
questions.evidence: I grew some lettuce and herbs on the balcony

explanation.en: He has never had a backyard; he grew lettuce and herbs in pots on the balcony of his old apartment.
explanation.ru: У него никогда не было своего двора («backyard»): он выращивал салат («lettuce») и зелень («herbs») в горшках («pots») на балконе («balcony») своей старой квартиры.
explanation.uk: У нього ніколи не було власного подвір’я («backyard»): він вирощував салат («lettuce») і зелень («herbs») у горщиках («pots») на балконі («balcony») своєї старої квартири.

questions.prompt: Main crop planned: ______
questions.evidence: So I'd say mainly peppers.

explanation.en: He thought about tomatoes but changed his mind, so he will grow mainly peppers.
explanation.ru: Он подумывал о помидорах («tomatoes»), но передумал, поэтому будет выращивать в основном перец («peppers»).
explanation.uk: Він думав про помідори («tomatoes»), але передумав, тож вирощуватиме переважно перець («peppers»).

questions.prompt: Orientation session: ______ at 9 a.m.
questions.evidence: The next one is Saturday morning at nine.

explanation.en: The Sunday afternoon session is already full, so he will go on Saturday morning at nine.
explanation.ru: На занятие в воскресенье днём («Sunday afternoon») мест уже нет, поэтому он пойдёт в субботу утром («Saturday morning») в девять («nine»).
explanation.uk: На заняття в неділю вдень («Sunday afternoon») місць уже немає, тож він піде в суботу вранці («Saturday morning») о дев’ятій («nine»).

parts.title: Changes to the Merrigal Heads coastal walk

turns.text: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming along. I'm Jacinta Rowley, a community officer with Merrigal Shire Council. Tonight I'll run through the changes we've made to the Merrigal Heads coastal walk, which fully reopens next month. You've got a map on your handout, so you can follow along.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Right, let's start at the main entrance at the southern end and imagine we're walking north. The main car park's on your left and the surf club's on your right. Now, lots of people have asked if the new toilets are inside the surf club. They're not. The toilet block is the building just past the surf club, still on your right, before you reach the junction.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Now, directly across from the toilets, on the other side of the path, you'll see something a lot of you asked for. So that's on your left, just north of the car park, and it's the new water refill station. It's got chilled drinking water and a low tap for dog bowls. Do use it, because there's no other water further along.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Okay, at the junction the coastal path turns right and heads east, while the bush track goes straight on north. Bikes aren't allowed on the coastal path any more, so we've put in bike racks. Go a few metres up the bush track and they're on your left, right against the edge of the Banksia Bushland. The little hut opposite them, on the right, is the old ranger's hut, and that's locked now.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Back on the coastal path, then, walking east. You'll pass the playground on your right-hand side. Opposite the playground, on your left, is our brand new picnic shelter, with six tables and two barbecues, which are free to use. You don't need to book them, just turn up.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Keep going past the playground, and on the same side, right at the corner where the path turns north, you'll find the first aid station. There's a defibrillator and a first aid kit, and surf club volunteers check it every week.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: From there the path follows the cliff top north to the headland. At the very end, on your right as you walk north, between the path and the ocean, is the new viewing platform. It's a great spot for whale watching from June. On your left at the end there's the old timber shelter, but that's coming down later this year, so please keep out of it.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Right, now closures. The old section that ran along the cliff edge past the blowhole has been closed for good. Some people think that's because of last winter's storm, and the storm didn't help, but the real reason is that the cliff is wearing away underneath. It's not about money, either. We had the budget to repair it, but our engineers said a path there simply isn't safe.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: There's also a temporary closure. We're resurfacing the stretch between the surf club and the junction, so that'll be shut for two weeks in May. Sorry, I tell a lie, it's June, starting on the 3rd. We'd first planned it for the school holidays, but we moved it so families wouldn't miss out.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: During those two weeks you can't walk from the car park to the rest of the path. And the bush track's no help, because you reach it from the same junction. Some people have suggested going along the beach instead, but at high tide that's really dangerous, so please don't. What we're doing instead is running a free shuttle bus from the car park to the picnic shelter every twenty minutes.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Now, dogs, which have caused a bit of debate. Dogs are still welcome, but they must be on a lead on the coastal path at all times. The one exception is the bush track, where they can be off the lead before nine in the morning. They're not allowed on the viewing platform, though.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: As for safety, you'd probably expect me to talk about falls, but in fact most of our call-outs are for heat. Every summer we get walkers with heat exhaustion, usually because they set off in the middle of the day. So my main advice is to start your walk early in the morning. And yes, wear a hat and decent shoes as well.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Finally, we'd love your feedback. The online survey actually closed last Friday, and we're not taking comments by email because they're too hard to keep track of. So the way to have your say now is to come to a drop-in session at Merrigal Library, on either the 14th or the 21st. Right, any questions?

parts.title: Discussing a language-app study

turns.text: Come in, Ben, have a seat. So, you've sent me the draft of your app study. How are you feeling about it?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Pretty good, mostly. Though it's changed quite a lot since the proposal.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Remind me where you started.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Well, originally I was going to look at the pronunciation feedback in the app, you know, where it records you saying a word in te reo Māori and gives you a score. But halfway through the semester the company took that feature out. I also thought about comparing beginners with advanced learners, but there weren't enough advanced ones. So in the end my question became whether the daily reminder notifications actually keep people practising.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Right. That's a sensible switch, and probably more interesting, to be honest. And who took part?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Twenty-two adults. I did think about asking first-years here at the university, but their timetables are all over the place. I also put a post on a couple of Facebook groups, but only three people replied. Most of them actually came from a night class at a community centre in Petone. The teacher there let me talk to the group.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Good. And what came out of it?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Well, I'd expected the younger learners to use it most, because they're on their phones all the time. But actually it was the people over fifty who opened the app most often. I hadn't predicted that at all. Plenty of people in both groups switched the notifications off at some point, but that wasn't really unusual.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Interesting. Now, you mentioned in your email that you were worried about the numbers.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Yeah, twenty-two seems tiny. I wondered if I should try to find another ten people before I hand it in.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Honestly, I wouldn't. Twenty-two is perfectly reasonable as long as you present it as an exploratory study. You're not claiming to speak for every learner in New Zealand, and that's fine.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: OK, that's a relief. The part I'm really struggling with is the discussion.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: In what way?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: It's not the length. I'm actually about four hundred words under the limit. And I think I can explain the odd result about age. It's more connecting what I found to the earlier research. Most of the studies I read were about apps for learning English, and I can't quite see how mine fits in.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: That's very common. Try picking two or three of those studies and saying directly whether your results agree or disagree with them. Now, what about the interviews you did?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: I've put them at the end, in a separate section. I wasn't sure they added much.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Oh, they do. I'd take some of the best quotes and put them right next to the numbers they relate to. So when you say the older group opened the app more, have someone explain why in their own words. It makes the figures much more convincing.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: That makes sense. So, what else do I need to add before I submit?
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: A few things. First, your appendix. You've included the questionnaire, which is good, but there's no copy of the consent form. The ethics committee will definitely want to see that.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Right, I'll put that in.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Next, the results. You've got the login figures for each age group in one big table, and it's quite hard to read. A bar chart would show the difference between the age groups at a glance.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: OK. I can do that in Excel easily enough.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Then in the methodology, you need to explain the timing. Your proposal said the study would run for eight weeks, but it actually ran for six weeks. Readers will want to know why.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: That was because the night class finished earlier than I'd been told. I'll explain that.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Good. And in the introduction, you describe the app quite briefly. Since your study is really about motivation, you should say more about its points system, how users earn points and lose them if they miss a day.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Fair enough. I sort of assumed everyone knew how it worked.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Not everyone's used it. Then there's the limitations section. You should be upfront about where your usage figures came from. The company wouldn't give you their data, would it?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: No, I asked twice. So everyone kept learning diaries, where they wrote down each time they used the app.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: Exactly, so say that clearly, because people don't always record things accurately.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Will do. And the deadline's the fourteenth, isn't it?
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: That was the original date, but it's been pushed back. The final version is now due on Friday 17 October, by five o'clock.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Great, that gives me a bit more breathing room. Thanks, Annabel.
turns.speaker: student

turns.text: No problem. Email me if you get stuck on the discussion.
turns.speaker: tutor

parts.title: Bioluminescence in the deep sea

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Dr Imogen Fairclough, and today we're continuing our series on life in the deep ocean. The topic is bioluminescence, that's the production of light by living things. I'll look first at how animals actually make light, then at why they do it, and finally at how scientists go about studying it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. Below about two hundred metres, sunlight fades almost completely, and yet something like three quarters of the animals living down there can produce their own light. So how do they do it? The process depends on a chemical called luciferin.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, a few species manufacture luciferin themselves, but a surprising number can't. Instead, they simply take it in through their diet, by eating smaller creatures that already contain it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Once the animal has the luciferin, it's stored in special light organs. You might expect these to be on the head or on the back, where they'd be easy to see. In fact, in most deep-sea fish they're arranged in rows along the belly, and we'll come back to why that is in a few minutes.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: When the animal wants to glow, a signal from its nerves triggers a reaction. The luciferin combines with an enzyme called luciferase. For a long time people assumed water was the third ingredient, but it's actually oxygen that's needed, and without it, no light is produced at all.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What comes out of this reaction is energy, released as light. And here's the remarkable part: almost none of it is lost as heat. Compare that with an old-fashioned light bulb, which wastes most of its energy warming up the room. That's why biologists often call this cold light.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The light organ itself is quite sophisticated. Behind the light there's usually a reflective layer that works rather like a mirror, sending the light outwards. And in front, many species have a lens, which focuses the light into a beam, a bit like the headlamp on a car.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What about colour? Coastal species, jellyfish near the shore for example, often glow green. But in the deep sea the light is nearly always blue, because blue light travels furthest through seawater. Red light, on the other hand, disappears very quickly.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, timing. Some animals glow steadily for hours, but most produce flashes, and a typical flash lasts less than a second. Short flashes save energy and make the animal much harder to locate.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK, so that's how. Now, why? The most common use is defence. Remember those lights along the belly?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Predators in the deep often swim below their prey and look upwards, watching for anything against the faint light from above. By glowing at just the right brightness, a fish can make its shadow disappear. We call this counter-illumination.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Light is also used for hunting. The anglerfish is the famous example, with its glowing lure that draws in curious prey. But personally, I find the dragonfish more interesting.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Unlike almost everything else down there, it produces red light, which most deep-sea animals can't see. So it works like a hidden torch, letting the dragonfish spot its victims without them noticing.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The third use is communication. Some small shrimps and fish flash in particular patterns, rather like a code. Researchers think the main purpose is to find a partner, although some patterns may also be warnings to rivals.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, the last section: how do we study all this? For most of the twentieth century, scientists relied on animals brought up in nets. The problem was that these delicate creatures were usually badly damaged on the way up, and many stopped producing light completely.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Nowadays, we use remotely operated vehicles, which are robots controlled from a ship. You might think they'd need powerful lights, but bright lights actually scare animals away, so researchers often switch them off. Instead, the vehicles are fitted with cameras so sensitive that they can pick up even the faintest glow.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And this research has benefits beyond marine biology. A glowing protein first found in a jellyfish is now used in hospitals and laboratories all over the world. Attaching it to cells allows doctors to watch how cancer spreads through the body, which has helped in developing new treatments.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, for next week, please read chapter six of the textbook, which covers vision in deep-sea animals. Thank you.
turns.speaker: lecturer

groups.title: How deep-sea animals produce light

questions.prompt: Many animals obtain luciferin through their ______ rather than making it.
questions.evidence: they simply take it in through their diet

explanation.en: The lecturer says only a few species make luciferin themselves; many get it from their diet by eating creatures that contain it.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что лишь немногие виды вырабатывают люциферин сами. Многие получают его с пищей, поедая существ, в организме которых он есть.
explanation.uk: Лекторка каже, що лише небагато видів виробляють люциферин самі. Багато хто отримує його з їжею, поїдаючи істот, в організмі яких він є.

questions.prompt: Luciferin is stored in light organs, usually in rows along the fish's ______.
questions.evidence: in most deep-sea fish they're arranged in rows along the belly

explanation.en: She says you might expect the organs on the head or back, but in most deep-sea fish they are along the belly.
explanation.ru: Она говорит, что эти органы можно было бы ожидать на голове или на спине, но у большинства глубоководных рыб они расположены вдоль брюха.
explanation.uk: Вона каже, що ці органи можна було б очікувати на голові чи на спині, але в більшості глибоководних риб вони розташовані вздовж черева.

questions.prompt: A nerve signal makes luciferin react with luciferase and ______.
questions.evidence: it's actually oxygen that's needed

explanation.en: People used to think water was the third ingredient, but the lecturer says it is really oxygen.
explanation.ru: Раньше считалось, что третий компонент — вода, но лектор говорит, что на самом деле это кислород ("oxygen").
explanation.uk: Раніше вважали, що третій компонент — вода, але лекторка каже, що насправді це кисень ("oxygen").

questions.prompt: Energy is released as light, with almost none lost as ______.
questions.evidence: almost none of it is lost as heat

explanation.en: Unlike an old light bulb, the reaction wastes almost no energy as heat, which is why it is called cold light.
explanation.ru: В отличие от старой лампочки накаливания, эта реакция почти не тратит энергию на тепло. Поэтому такой свет и называют холодным ("cold light").
explanation.uk: На відміну від старої лампи розжарювання, ця реакція майже не витрачає енергії на тепло. Тому таке світло й називають холодним ("cold light").

questions.prompt: A ______ at the front of the organ concentrates the light into a beam.
questions.evidence: in front, many species have a lens, which focuses the light into a beam

explanation.en: The mirror-like layer is behind the light; the part in front that focuses the light is a lens.
explanation.ru: Зеркальный слой находится позади источника света, а часть спереди, которая фокусирует свет, — это линза ("lens").
explanation.uk: Дзеркальний шар розташований позаду джерела світла, а частина спереду, що фокусує світло, — це лінза ("lens").

questions.prompt: The light is usually ______, as this colour travels furthest in seawater.
questions.evidence: in the deep sea the light is nearly always blue

explanation.en: Green light is common in coastal species, and red disappears quickly; deep-sea light is nearly always blue.
explanation.ru: Зелёный свет часто встречается у прибрежных видов, а красный быстро исчезает. На глубине же свет почти всегда синий ("blue").
explanation.uk: Зелене світло часто трапляється в прибережних видів, а червоне швидко зникає. На глибині ж світло майже завжди синє ("blue").

groups.title: Why animals produce light and how it is studied

questions.prompt: Defence: lights on the underside stop predators below from seeing the animal's ______
questions.evidence: a fish can make its shadow disappear

explanation.en: Predators look up from below, so by glowing at the right brightness a fish makes its shadow disappear.
explanation.ru: Хищники смотрят снизу вверх, поэтому рыба, светясь с нужной яркостью, делает свою тень невидимой.
explanation.uk: Хижаки дивляться знизу вгору, тому риба, світячись із потрібною яскравістю, робить свою тінь невидимою.

questions.prompt: Hunting: the dragonfish's red light acts as a hidden ______
questions.evidence: So it works like a hidden torch

explanation.en: The anglerfish uses a lure, but the dragonfish's red light, which other animals can't see, works like a hidden torch.
explanation.ru: Удильщик использует приманку, а красный свет рыбы-дракона, которого другие животные не видят, работает как скрытый фонарик.
explanation.uk: Вудильник використовує приманку, а червоне світло риби-дракона, якого інші тварини не бачать, діє як прихований ліхтарик.

questions.prompt: Communication: flashing patterns are mainly used to find a ______
questions.evidence: the main purpose is to find a partner

explanation.en: Some patterns may warn rivals, but researchers think the main purpose is finding a partner.
explanation.ru: Некоторые узоры, возможно, служат предупреждением для соперников, но исследователи считают, что их главная цель — поиск партнёра.
explanation.uk: Деякі візерунки, можливо, слугують попередженням для суперників, але дослідники вважають, що їхня головна мета — пошук партнера.

questions.prompt: Early research: animals brought up in ______ were often badly damaged
questions.evidence: scientists relied on animals brought up in nets

explanation.en: In the twentieth century animals were collected in nets and were usually damaged on the way up.
explanation.ru: В двадцатом веке животных ловили сетями, и при подъёме на поверхность они обычно получали повреждения.
explanation.uk: У двадцятому столітті тварин збирали сітками, і під час підйому на поверхню вони зазвичай зазнавали пошкоджень.
